**The spontaneity of the Lord: the self-aware light**

This is where the whole Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī begins — with the spontaneity, the
svācchandya, of the Lord. And the doctrine is announced in its fullness from the first lines. The blue
and the yellow and the jar are not things that a light shines upon from outside; they shine forth
*as* the light, without abandoning their own being, and are one with the manifestation itself. This —
that the world shines as the consciousness, and that the consciousness shines as the world — is the
Lord's spontaneity.

The Lord is of the nature of consciousness. He shines forth as the whole variety of knowers and knowns,
with a body that appears as if it were more than consciousness even though it is not more; and — this is
decisive — he is *aware* of shining. The image Abhinavagupta uses is the mirror. A mirror reflects the
wall, the house, the elephant, the horse, the person, the pot, the potter — all the distinctions of
part and whole, support and supported, cause and effect — without being more than its own smooth
surface. But the mirror does not know that it reflects. That is its only limit; it is inert. The Lord
is the mirror that *knows*: he shines forth as all things, and he is aware that he does so, because
consciousness culminates in reflexive-awareness. The light that shines is the light that knows itself
shining.

And this answers the obvious objection: "then it would always shine." For the "always" has no
independent time against which it could fail. What we call time is just the sun's movement — the
shining of things in their succession. To ask "why does the world shine as the sun moves?" is like
asking "why does the blue not shine as yellow?" It is the nature of the light to shine; there is no
time outside it that could make it shine or not. So the Lord is: *śaśvat*, un-cut by time; *acchanna*,
never becoming other than his own form; *svaccha*, clear — able to appear as more than himself while
being only himself; and *svacchanda*, spontaneous — free of all dependence on another, resting in his
own pulsation.

And so the opening of the work is a prostration. The author bows to Śiva — the param-eśvara who removes
the delusion of the world, who is the essence of all good, the bliss and the liberation. And the
prostration, Abhinavagupta explains, is not an empty word. It is the samāveśa, the entry: the
abandoning of the bound knower's conceit, the subordination of the "I" of the world, and the rising of
the self-aware consciousness. Even the word "namaḥ," the bowing, does its work not by being offered as
a bare sound but by pleasing the Lord — as the oblation's svāhā kindles the flame and gives to the
deity.

So the whole teaching is here, in the first opening: the Lord is the self-aware light, the mirror that
knows, the spontaneity that shines as the world and is aware of shining; and the recognition of this —
the entry into this self-aware Śiva — is the whole of the liberation the work will unfold.

  whole, support/supported, cause/effect); the mirror's un-awareness as its inertia; the param-eśvara

[chunk-b-eligibility-gita-v2] Dyczkowski-mode.*

**The homage that is two-resting, and who is worthy to make it**

The work opens with a prostration — and Abhinavagupta takes care to say what that prostration is. It
is not a bending of the body, nor an empty sound. It is a *two-resting* homage: it rests at once in the
Lord, whom it exalts, and in the devotee, whom it subordinates. The words of homage — "jaya," "victory,"
"namaḥ," "I bow," "I worship" — all move by one of these two directions, but each must culminate in the
other. The "victory" of the Lord, to be real, requires the devotee's self-subordination; the "I bow" of
the devotee, to be real, must rest in the Lord's excess. The two — the exalting and the subordinating —
are one act, two aspects, made manifest by the single word of homage before the whole assembly.

And the attaining of the Lord, the commentary tells us, is the attainment of *dāsya* — of
servant-ness. And the servant-ness is extremely hard to get: that is what "kathaṃcit," "in some way,"
means. It is not a title; it is the very heart of the eligibility. And it is fruitful of the greatest
good — for in becoming the servant of the Lord one attains the Lord's own excess, and all the fortunes
(dāsyalakṣmī) follow from that servant-ness, granted by the Lord's grace. It is this that makes the
devotee one who has attained all.

The homage, moreover, is made in the mind and the speech — the mind-awareness and the word-essence —
never in the inert body. "Even by speech," the text says, and by the "even" we understand "and by the
body." But the prostration proper is the offering of the undivided mind-and-speech, which is the
consciousness-power itself; and in offering that, the devotee offers the whole world to the Lord. As the
teaching says: "he should offer his own self." The physical prostration — the bowing, the eight-limbed
salutation — is only the upacāra, the visible mark by which the inner offering is inferred, not the
primary act.

And so the question of who is worthy. The objection arises: "the eligibility suits the explainer, who
has attained; but how does it suit the mere listeners?" Abhinavagupta's answer is that the listener and
the explainer are not two separate undertakings: the recognition is one, and the servant-ness is one. It
is by this that the Lord's favor is won — the recognition is preceded by, and inferred from, the Lord's
favor. And this is where the Gītā's four kinds of devotees come in — the distressed, the seeker of
knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the knower. All of them, in their several gradations, are worthy of
the servant-ness and of the recognition. The door is not narrow in the way of the world's ranks; it is
narrow only in the way of the heart — for what is required is the self-subordination, the dāsya, and
that, once attained, draws the Lord near.

  the attainment of all fortunes (dāsyalakṣmī, by the Lord's grace); "vācāpi" = by body too; the

  self"; the physical prostration as the upacāra (inferred mark); the "satyam" (obstacle-removal vs.
  the greater purpose); "adyāpi" (un-broken, by the book); the explainer honored; the recognition
  preceded by the Lord's favor; the listener-not-separate objection and answer; the four Gītā-devotees

[chunk-c-svatma-maya-upanishad-v3] Dyczkowski-mode.*

**The own-self: the one consciousness, whose body is the world**

The kārikā says that the own-self alone is the Lord. But what is this "own-self"? Does it reach the
whole world — the inert things, the void, everything? The objector presses hard on this. If the
maheśvara is the self of the blue, then he must be the self of the yellow too; and then how can the
world be divided — "this is the blue, this is the yellow"? The answer turns on what "own-self" really
means.

The "own" in "own-self" (svātmā) is not restricted to anything in particular; so it is the self's own —
the inner, non-other-dependent, un-conditioned relation. And what is that? It is consciousness. For
the conscious things, he is plainly the one self. But for the inert — the lump of clay, the blue — how
can they have one self, since separate things seem to have separate natures? Here Abhinavagupta shows
that the inert, in its supposed inertia, has no real being at all. If the clay is truly in itself, is
it or is it not? If it were not, nothing would suffer; if it did its effect, so what; if it shone,
what is its own glory? The "it shines for me, for Caitra" fails too — for the perception belongs to
the perceiver, not to the thing; and "by the perceiver it shines" is a new-fangled reason that would
make the white make the yellow white. In truth, the thing has no being apart from its being-manifested;
and being-manifested is the consciousness's own act. So the blue and the yellow are not things with
their own separate bodies; they are *awareness-forms* (bodhātmānaḥ) — and their own-self, no less than
ours, is the maheśvara.

What of the void, the mere nothing? If it is cognized at all, then the maheśvara is its self too; if
it is not cognized, then it is nothing, and no one's self is at issue. The test is always the same: is
it cognized? That is the whole answer — the "being-cognized" is what makes anything the self of the
one consciousness.

And so the division of the world. If the maheśvara is the self of the blue and of the yellow alike,
how is "this is the blue, this is the yellow" possible? Abhinavagupta's answer is that the division is
not a division of the self. The whole known world is the *body* of the consciousness-self. Just as my
body, though an object of my knowledge, is nonetheless "I" — not metaphorically, but literally, by the
un-abandoned support of the self — so the whole world is "I" to the consciousness. The body's being
"I" is no mere figure of speech (as when we call a tool by its owner's name); even those who think
themselves quite separate from one another feel the body as "I." So the consciousness is
world-form (viśvarūpā); the blue and the yellow are not cut off from it as from a thing outside, but
are its very forms, as the space of the jar and the space of the cloth are the one space.

The upshot: the own-self is the one consciousness, whose body is the whole world. The blue and the
yellow, the inert and the void, are all awareness-forms; their own-self is the maheśvara. The division
of the world is the division of what appears within the one light, not a split in the light itself.
And this one — the knower, the doer, the self of all — is the Lord: the jñātṛ-kartṛ, who knows and
acts, and whose very being is to be the self of everything.

  have him as the one self; the inert's being/non-being difficulty; the "it shines for me/for Caitra"
  failure; the "by the perceiver it shines" as an un-precedented reason (white makes yellow white);
  the thing's no-being apart from its manifestation; the identity of being with the consciousness as
  the pervader; the blue/yellow as awareness-forms, their self the maheśvara; the void (cognized → the
  maheśvara's self; un-cognized → nothing); the "being-cognized" as the answer; the world as the body
  of the consciousness; the body's "I" as un-metaphorical (not the upacāra of a tool); the
  consciousness as world-form; the ghaṭākāśa/paṭākāśa (the one space) citation.

[chunk-d-memory-pramana-v4] Dyczkowski-mode.*

**The eternal knower: "I was never not"**

Memory seems to bind the self to the past — to what the self has itself experienced. But then the
objection arises, and it is a sharp one. "I was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa," the reader says.
"Vālmīki composed it long ago, and I was not there to experience it; so how can the self, which
remembers only what it has experienced, be the eternal knower?"

Abhinavagupta answers that the objection mistakes the body for the self. It is true that *this body*
was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa — but that is not the self. The "I"-recollection, the aham-vimarśa,
is of the consciousness-nature, and it is eternal. And here is the crucial move: if memory reaches only
what has been experienced, then even the Vālmīki of the Rāmāyaṇa was an experiencer; and the āgama
itself, by which we learn of that time, presupposes an experiencer. What flashes in the "we were not" —
the past-time-appearance, in the perfect tense — is itself a cognition; and since it is not the
experience-form (else the past would flash like the yogin's present), it must be memory. And memory, by
its very nature, presupposes a prior experience. So every memory, even the memory of the Rāmāyaṇa, points
back to an experiencer who was there.

This is where the eternal knower enters. The pure consciousness-mere, being free of the tint of time,
cannot by itself bear the memory; the memory is of the body-and-the-rest-tinted. But the tint of the
prior body is distinct from the tint of this body — so the memory-ness, if pinned to the body, would not
be clear (as the young man who was never a child would have no clear memory of childhood). The clear
memory requires the firm conceit of the experiencer — and that conceit, in its root, is the self that
was there. And that self, being consciousness, is not cut by time.

So the manifestation of the self is not un-precedented (apūrva). It does not begin to shine at some
moment; it was always shining. The being-ness of the self rests in its manifestation, and its being was
never otherwise. Hence the "un-precedented manifestation" (apūrva-prakāśa) that we seem to see — the
new appearance of things in time — presupposes, and rests upon, the eternal knower. The body's
appearance is un-precedented, but only against the background of the eternal, always-manifested
param-essence knower. And that knower is the param-eśvara, who is never un-precedented in his
manifestation; and all the knowers are un-divided from him. So, in truth, there is no un-precedented
manifestation at all.

This is the point of the Gītā verse that Abhinavagupta cites: "For truly I was never not… nor shall
we not be." The self — the param-essence knower — is un-cut by all three times: past, present, and
future. It did not come into being, and it will not pass away. And because all the knowers are one
with it, the same is true, in the deepest sense, of them all. The un-precedented manifestation may
appear in the māyā-bound knower, but it rests in the eternal knower. The pramāṇa — the valid means by
which we know — is thus grounded, in the end, in this one eternal knower, who was never not, and who is
the self of all.

  āgama presupposing the experiencer; the aham-vimarśa as eternal; the body-was-not vs. the
  self-was-not; the dissolution/creation "we were not"; the liṭ (perfect) past-appearance flashing;
  memory (not the experience-form) presupposing the prior experience; the utprekṣā rooted in
  memory/experience; the pure consciousness free of time-tint not bearing memory alone; the
  body-and-the-rest tint; the prior/this-body tint distinction (the young man never a child); the
  firm-conceit requirement; the self's manifestation not un-precedented; the apūrva-prakāśa resting in

  Gītā 2.12; the māyā-knower's apūrva-prakāśā resting in the eternal; the pramāṇa grounded in the
  eternal knower.

[chunk-e-cit-acid-dvairasya-v5] Dyczkowski-mode.*

**The self is the Lord: what the recognition does**

The kārikā declares that the self alone is the Lord. And at once a sharp objection arises. A valid
means of knowledge, it is said, establishes what was *not* established before — it serves the practical
dealings of the world. But the Lord-self, on our own showing, is already established. So what could a
pramāṇa possibly do here? What is there left for it to prove?

Abhinavagupta's answer turns this objection around. For an inert object, even an established one, the
pramāṇa does indeed make a new attainment — it brings out some part that was not yet grasped, at least
the manifestation and the designation (prakhyā and upākhyā) of the thing in our dealing with it. But in
the self — the Lord — there is nothing un-attained to be established. The manifestation and the
designation are already there; without them, not even a trace of a thing could be known at all. So the
pramāṇa here is not establishing something new.

What, then, is it doing? It is *foregrounding* what is already present but hidden. The recognition
(pratyabhijñā) does not bring the Lord into being; it brings the Lord, who was always near and always
present, into the *foreground of our own awareness*. As Abhinavagupta says, what is hidden and standing
close by is shown as primary, by the coming-together of the heart. The recognition makes the
manifestation and the designation of the self-as-Lord no longer an instrument lost among the things of
the body and the world, but the primary thing that we see. It is the turning of the attention — the
"see, see" — upon what was always before us.

And this recognition is the very content of the whole teaching. After the upoddhāta, the opening, the
whole śāstra that is to come has, as its to-be-said content, the recognition — which is the
jñāna-kriyā, the knowledge-and-action power, made firm by the conviction (dṛḍhaniścaya) that arises from
it. The two powers — knowledge and action — are determined at length throughout the work, and the firm
conviction in the self-as-Lord is their fruit.

So the point is this: the self is the Lord, and he is already established — not to be newly proved, but
to be *recognized*. The pramāṇa does not reach out to a distant, un-known thing; it turns the light of
attention upon the one who was always the knower and the known, the one standing near in the very act
of knowing. The recognition is not the acquisition of something new; it is the foregrounding of the
self, the Lord, who was never absent. And this, the firm conviction in the self-as-Lord, is what the
whole teaching sets before us.

**The self is the Lord: against the Buddhist no-self**

The upoddhāta, the preliminary of the whole work, must first clear the ground — by showing who denies
the self's lordship and why their denial fails. Not everyone is a real opponent. The materialist, the
Cārvāka, cannot even argue: having no means of proof of their own, they cannot refute the other side
without first adopting the very conventions of proof they reject. The Sāṃkhya, with its many selves or
its one self with hidden lordship, is not wholly far from us. The real opponent — the one who must be
met head-on — is the **Buddhist**, the Sautrāntika, who denies the self outright. It is his no-self that
the eleven verses of this vimarśa set out and answer.

The Buddhist's attack is twofold. First, he denies the self that we claim to perceive: "the self is
not seen," he says, "only the momentary cognitions flash by, with their own-mark appearances." Second,
he denies the self that we might infer: memory and the synthesis, he holds, are otherwise established —
they are only the work of the impressions in the stream, with no abiding owner behind them. So the
self, whether taken as perceived or as inferred, is rejected; and with it, he concludes, the whole
apparatus of the knowledge-action relation — the very lordship we ascribe to the self — collapses, for
there is no one to be the knower and the doer.

Abhinavagupta meets him on both fronts. To the denial of the perceived self, he answers with the
"I"-cognition itself (ahaṃpratyaya): the self is not some object hidden behind the perceptions — it is
present, unmistakably, in the very act of saying "I." The "I" is not a thing seen among others; it is
the seeing itself, that which is present in every cognition, never itself absent. The ādi — the stream
of the senses, the breath, the knowledge — all presuppose this "I" that runs through them. The Buddhist's
"the self is not seen" fails: the self is the seer, and the seer is never not seen, for he is the
seeing.

And the memory and the synthesis, far from being otherwise established, themselves require the abiding
self. A memory reaches across the break of experience and says "I saw this before" — and only an
abiding self could hold the before and the after together in the single "I." The stream of moments
cannot do this; moments have no thread by which to re-collect. So memory and the synthesis, which the
Buddhist thought freed him from the self, in truth demand the self. And the knowledge-action relation —
the knowing and the doing — is precisely this self's lordship: the one who knows and the one who acts
is the self, and that is what it is to be the Lord.

So the upoddhāta's defense is complete in outline. The Cārvāka cannot argue, the Sāṃkhya is near; the
real opponent, the Buddhist no-self, is met and answered. The self is established even by the
"I"-cognition; memory and the synthesis require the abiding self; and the knowledge-action relation —
the knowing and the doing of the one who says "I" — is the self's lordship. The self is real, and the
self is the Lord.

**The cognition cannot be a thing: the dilemma of the consciousness-form**

The Buddhist had denied the self. But he had also, in a different mood, offered a reason for the
self's lordship — "by the union of knowledge and action." To stop even this, Abhinavagupta turns the
same logic against the cognition itself. Whatever the opponent says cognition is, it cannot stand.
And he forces the choice with a single dilemma, put in the seventh kārikā: if the cognition is of the
consciousness-form, then it must be eternal, like the self; but if it is inert, then it cannot reveal
any object at all. There is no third option.

Take the first horn. The consciousness-nature is, by its very marker, *self-manifestation* — it is the
light that knows itself. And self-manifestation is directly opposed to being-an-object, to being
manifested by another. A thing that is manifest by another is caught in place and time — it is here or
there, now or then. But the self-manifest light is free of all such being-caught. If the cognition were
truly of the consciousness-form, it could not be the momentary, place-and-time-bound thing the Buddhist
takes it to be; it would have to be eternal and omnipresent, exactly like the self. And then the
Buddhist's whole picture — a stream of fleeting cognitions, each a separate momentary quality — falls
apart. The cognition would not be a momentary flash; it would be the eternal light itself.

The Buddhist tries to escape by saying: "the cognition is not the self's own form; it is a quality of
the self, made by the union with the mind." But this, Abhinavagupta shows, fails too. For what we call
the cognition is the manifestation of the blue and the rest; and if that manifestation is only an
occasional quality, absent when its cause is absent, then the self, apart from it, is simply not
manifesting the blue. The cognition, taken as a separate thing, has no place to stand. Whether you call
it consciousness-form or a quality, it dissolves.

The second horn is no better. If the cognition is inert — a dead thing, like the objects — then how
could it reveal anything? An inert thing does not shine; it is shone upon. It cannot be the
manifestation of the blue, for manifestation is not a property of the inert. So the inert cognition
cannot account for the one thing it is supposed to explain — the appearing of objects.

And beneath both horns lies a deeper point. If the cognition were a separate thing, caught in place and
time, it would have to be held and supported by something; but the self-manifest light cannot be held
or covered by another — the covered thing, we might say, could not bear another's support. So the whole

**Enjoyment is the meeting of two reflections**

What is it to enjoy — to experience an object? The schools have their answers: the Sāṃkhya makes the
cognition a transformation of matter; the Vaiśeṣika makes it a quality of the self joined to the object
by a mysterious relation called inherence (samavāya). Abhinavagupta cuts through all of this with a
single image: enjoyment is the *union of two reflections* — the reflection of consciousness and the
reflection of the object — meeting in the intellect, and fused by the ego into the one act "I know
this."

Consider what happens when you know the blue. The intellect (buddhi) bears two reflections: the
reflection of consciousness — the light itself, as it is present in the act of knowing — and the
reflection of the blue, the object. The ego (ahaṅkāra) mixes them into the single conceit "I know
this," and that conceit — the two reflections joined, determined by the intellect, resting in the one
consciousness — is the enjoyment. The self, in itself, is not really an enjoyer; it is
consciousness-mere. It is the ego that makes it appear as one who enjoys. And this is not a mere figure
of speech in the loose sense: if it were, then by the infinite division of knowers, the same body could
be dealt with at once as fire and water, as contradictory things, in a single moment — which is absurd.
The enjoyment is real, but real as this union of reflections in the one consciousness.

Now the Vaiśeṣika says: the cognition is a quality of the self, and it is joined to the object by
inherence (samavāya). But Abhinavagupta's point is that the mere *relation* does all the work. If the
cognition-quality is other than the self, then how is it enjoyed? "By inherence," the Vaiśeṣika says.
But then the relation alone is the cause of the enjoyment-form — and that is precisely our point. Here
too there is a relation: the consciousness-reflection, the object-reflection, the ego's mixing, the
intellect's determining — the union in the one support. And the union is enough. Whether you call it
conjunction (saṃyoga) or inherence (samavāya) matters not at all; once the thing is understood, the
word is a mere label. And if the conjunction's beginning is not to be found in the prior dissolutions,
then the conjunction, being beginningless, is not distinct from the inherence. Either way, in every
view, the enjoyment-dealing is *relation-made* — saṃsargakṛta.

So the deep point is this. Enjoyment is not a transaction between a self and a thing across a gap; it
is the meeting, within the one light, of the light and the object's reflection, fused by the ego into
"I know this." The relation — whatever we name it — is the whole of it. And this is why the 
consciousness-reflection and the object-reflection, wherever they meet in the intellect, stand in the
support-supported relation, even to the point where one might call it inherence — without any
contradiction. The enjoyment of the world is, in the end, the self-luminous light meeting its own
reflections in the one act of knowing.

**Action is the ordered operation, not a thing that moves**

The opponent had offered the self's lordship as the union of knowledge and action. We have seen that
knowledge cannot be a separate thing in his view. Now Abhinavagupta shows that *action* cannot be a
separate thing either. Kārikā 9 makes the point: the action of a body is just the coming-to-be of this
or that place; it is not some hidden cause (the unseen, adṛṣṭa) moving it; and it is not one — for
order does not belong to a single thing.

But wait — if action is not a movement, what is it? The word-knowers, the grammarians, refuse to say
that the body-less self moves. They locate the self's agency only in the union of knowledge, desire,
and effort. So the action that belongs to the self must be defined differently. Its marker,
Abhinavagupta says, is this: the operation of the agent that brings about the fruit — the means,
related to the doer, or inhering in it, or its very self — whose form is such that its parts are
prior-and-later, standing in order. Action is the ordered operation. And the gurus' verses make this
vivid: "as long as the established or un-established is spoken of as the to-be-established, being of
the resting-order-form, it is perceived as that action." The mass of order-born parts, unified by the
mind, is what we call action. "White is whitened" — the whiteness appears as a prior-later order, and
that is the declaration of action. So action is not a thing that moves; it is the ordered self-shaping
of a nature.

And this action is in the self. "He desires, he knows, he strives" — these are the prior-later dharmas
of the one self, perceived in their order; and this ordered operation, Abhinavagupta notes, is accepted
by the very thinkers who hold the self to be the Lord. The guru's words: "such is the will, such the
knowledge, such the action." The will, the knowledge, the action — these are not three separate things
attached to a self; they are the one self's ordered operation, its desiring and knowing and striving,
held together as the single action.

So the action, like the cognition, cannot be broken into momentary flashes or hidden causes. It is the
one, ordered operation of the self — the will that knows and acts. And this is why the union of
knowledge and action is not a reason that the opponent can offer for lordship; it is the self's own
nature. The self that desires, knows, and strives — in that single ordered act — is the Lord. The
union of knowledge and action is not a quality added to the self; it is the self, shining as the 
ordered operation of the one who wills and knows and does.

[chunk-j-k1-11-kartapi-kalpita-v10] **"Thence the agent too is constructed"**

The Buddhist's attack has been relentless. He has denied the self, denied the cognition, denied the
action. Now he completes it. For what holds all these together — the *relation* between the knower and
the known, between the agent and the act — is itself impossible; and once the relation is gone, "thence
the agent too is constructed." The agent, like everything else, is only a fabrication, a convenient
construction with nothing real behind it.

The kārikā's "thence" gathers a fourfold absence as its reason: the absence of the action, the absence
of the object, the absence of the relation, and the absence of any determination of being in any of
them. And the relation's absence is argued on its own terms. A relation would have to stand *in both*
its terms — in the knower and the known at once. But the two-resting thing cannot be one: what stands
in two cannot be a single thing, any more than the two jars in the two houses are one jar. Moreover,
the established does not expect another — a thing already complete does not reach out for a relation —
and the dependence that a relation would impose is itself unfitting. So the relation is absent; and
with it, the agent that the relation would bind together is only constructed.

Abhinavagupta pauses to make one methodological point, and it is important. The Buddhist thinks he
refutes the relation by a bare non-perception — "I do not see it, so it is not." But a bare
non-perception proves non-being only within a restriction of place and time: "here, now, there is no
jar." It cannot reach the universal non-being of the relation. To do that, one must show a real
contradiction in the opponent's own account — that the very form he ascribes to the relation is
contradicted by another form he ascribes to it. That is a refutation grounded in the thing itself
(prameya-niṣṭha), not a mere failure to perceive.

And this is where the pūrvapakṣa — the no-self attack — comes to its close. The Buddhist has shown,
to his own satisfaction, that the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation all fall; and
"thence the agent too is constructed." The whole edifice of a real knower and doer is, for him, a
fabrication.

**The reply: the cognition is self-cognition**

The Buddhist's attack has run its course — the self, the cognition, the action, the relation all
denied, and "thence the agent too is constructed." Now, in the third vimarśa, the established doctrine
replies. And Abhinavagupta's first move is a shrewd concession. "It is true," he begins — and this is
the characteristic gesture of the reflective thinker, granting the opponent what is sound in order to
sharpen what is not. It is true, he says, that the cognition cannot be a separate thing in the way the
Sāṃkhya or the Kāṇāda suppose; that much the Buddhist has rightly seen. But — and here is the turn — the
reason the cognition cannot be a separate thing is precisely because it is *self-cognition*
(svasaṃvid). It is not a quality attached to a self; it is the self's own luminous awareness of itself.
And this self-cognition is the very self the Buddhist thought he had abolished.

Consider memory. When you remember, the prior experience does not stand before you as a new object; it
shines in the single act of the "I" that remembers. The cognition, even in memory, is self-cognition —
it is aware of itself, not of some detached past thing. The Buddhist thought memory freed him from the
self; but memory itself is self-luminous. And if the construction, the determination, were all error —
as the Buddhist would have it — then every determination would fall, and the dealing of the world would
collapse. The Buddhist cannot have it both ways. The memory, the determination, the cognition all
presuppose the self-luminous awareness that is aware of itself in each act.

So the siddhānta's reply rests on the self-luminous dṛk — the seeing that is aware of itself. The "I"
is not constructed; it is that without which no cognition, no memory, no construction could shine at
all. The cognition is self-cognition: it is the light that knows itself, and this light is the self —
the self that the Buddhist denied and Abhinavagupta here restores. And because this self-cognition is
self-luminous and free, it is the Lord. The one who is aware of himself in every act of knowing is the
one who knows and acts — the self, the Lord, whose cognition is his self-cognition and whose power
reaches through the whole of memory and action.

The jñāna-vicāra — the examination of the cognition — thus begins the reply. The Buddhist is granted
his insight (the cognition is not a separate thing) and then outflanked: it is not a thing because it
is the self-luminous awareness, which is the self. From here the siddhānta will build — showing that
this self-cognition is the memory, the power of removal, and ultimately the Lord who knows and acts.

**The self-luminous seeing: how the yogin knows another's mind**

We have said the cognition is self-cognition, and the self is self-luminous. But this seems to close
the door on a striking fact — the yogin's knowledge of another's mind. If the self is not an object,
how can the yogin perceive another's cognition with perfect clarity? And if the cognition is
self-luminous only in its own stream, could it not, after all, be manifested by some other cognition?

The answer to the first is that the yogin's knowledge of another is a *perception*, not an inference.
It is the yogipratyakṣa. By the discipline of the yogin — the holding, the meditating, the samādhi —
one comes, in the union with the other, to meditate the non-difference of the self from the other. And
that meditation, following the truth of the thing (for in truth there is unity, and the conceit of
difference is māyā-made), makes the other's cognition shine forth directly, clearly, as a thing seen —
not inferred, not concluded. As the yoga-sūtra says, the knowledge of another's cognition comes by the
saṃyama. The other's passions, too, are manifested in this seeing; but in their very experience the
yogin and the other are one, so the experience shines as self-luminous, not as an object spread before
a detached observer.

And this is the point that matters. The other's cognition, thus seen, is a direct seeing
(sākṣātkāra) — not a conclusion about another stream. And the self that sees, and the self that is
seen, are, in that act, one. So the "being-manifested-by-another" — the picture of one cognition
standing as an object before another — has no place even here. The other knower too is not manifested
by another; he is self-luminous, and in the yogin's perception the two are one.

Now the second objection: "the cognition is self-luminous in its own stream, but could it not, with
respect to another knower, be manifested by another cognition? After all, the same woman gives pleasure
to her lover and pain to her rival — the same thing, different effects, no contradiction." Abhinavagupta
answers with the unity of the knower: "he experienced, I have experienced." The self-cognition rests in
the one knower. The "he" and the "I" are not two streams that might objectify each other; they are the
one self, which remembers its own experience. The cognition is not a thing to be passed from one stream
to another as an object; it is the one self-luminous awareness, aware of itself, and of nothing
else as an object.

So the dṛk — the seeing — is self-manifest alone. It is never the object of another cognition, because
it is the very light in which all cognitions shine, and it is one. The yogin's perception of another is
not the exception that breaks this; it is its confirmation — for in that perception, the two are one,
and the other's cognition is the yogin's own self-luminous awareness. And the Buddhist's picture of
separate streams, each objectifying the other, is refuted. The seeing is self-luminous; the self is
one; and this self-luminous, one seeing is the self — and the Lord.

**The determination cannot reach outside**

The Buddhist, having lost the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation, falls back on one
last notion: the *determination* (adhyavasāya) — the act by which, he thinks, the cognition is taken
to establish an external thing. Abhinavagupta now cuts this last thread. The determination, he shows,
cannot establish anything outside.

Consider how the "external" seems to appear. It is, Abhinavagupta says, only the strength of the firm
practice-impression that makes the appearance seem drawn to an external object. From the very first,
the appearance shining in the consciousness and in the determination is taken as external — but only
for the slow-minded, in the illusion and the diseased-eye case. He who knows the cause of the
appearance does not determine its externality at all. The child who cries in astonishment, "the trees
on the far bank rush against the current!" is told: "it is not so — the trees do not rush; it is only
seen so." The manifestation-dharma alone is this. The seeming outwardness is a manner of the seeing,
not a thing established.

And the determination itself, Abhinavagupta presses, is error-form. In every determination — even in
the most ordinary case — there is this error-form, this drawing of the appearance outward. So the
external, which the error-form determination was supposed to establish, has no standing in that very
part: for the part is inert, and an inert thing cannot establish. And in the part that is not inert —
the non-construction, the pure self-experience — there the establishment is not made either, for that
part shines only its own form and its own self-appearance. So the determination's object-establishing
power fails on both sides. The non-erroneous part, the self-experience, is un-divided from the
memory-cognition — it is not a separate thing reaching out to an external — and so it is not
external-natured.

The Buddhist tries once more: "let the determination be both erroneous and establishing — what is the
harm?" But this too fails, for the reason is the inertness: an inert thing cannot establish. And the
last attempt — "as the fire burns the wood though inert, so the determination establishes the object;
why this question of inert or conscious?" — is met: the establishing is in the self; the experience,
with the manifestation at its head, is the establishing, and it is self-luminous, not a thing that
reaches a thing.

So the whole attempt to find a real external established by the determination collapses. The
determination is only the manifestation-form in the self; the external is only drawn-to by the
impression, never established; and the self-experience, un-divided from the memory-cognition, is the
self-luminous awareness alone. The cognition never establishes a thing outside itself, because there
is nothing outside the self-luminous awareness for it to reach. The self is one, self-luminous, and
all — the memory, the determination, the experience — are its own shining.

**The one who is the whole world: the close of the first volume**

The cognitions, we have seen, are self-luminous and one with the "I." But how, the question arises, do
they not take the form of the "I" when they appear as the objects — the blue, the yellow, the jar? The
answer is that their seeming excess over the "I" — their non-pervasion, their non-eternity, their being
caught in the place and time of the object — is made only by the object-facing condition (upādhi). The
difference of the object, Abhinavagupta says, is a mere conceit (abhimāna), made by the māyā-power; and
even in the state of māyā, the deep un-dividedness of the object from the "I" is un-broken. For māyā is
the Lord's own power — and a power does not cover the power-holder. The māyā cannot hide the Lord's own
form, because it is his own shining. So the whole world, even the seemingly external, is un-divided
from the "I": the one whose body is consciousness, with the inner-made, infinite world-form, possessed
of the knowledge and the rest of the powers.

This is the great vision toward which the volume has been building. The Lord is the one whose body is
the whole world — the inner-made, the outer-form, all of it, un-lost in the least, made by his freedom
and resting in the one knower. The world, counted in the four, the six, the sixteen, the twenty-four,
the thirty-six categories and more, is his body. There is nothing outside the consciousness; the māyā
is his power, not a veil over him.

And the synthesis (anusandhāna) — the act by which the many cognitions are gathered into one — is
itself the consciousness. The objection: "you said the memory's arising is the world's standing; but
here you say 'if the synthesis were not,' and call it consciousness-form — how?" Abhinavagupta answers:
the synthesis of all the knowledges, mutually, *is* the consciousness-tattva. By the co-reference, by
the following-ness, the one-becoming of even the seemingly separate cognitions is the consciousness
alone, turned inward — nothing else. The mixer of the fragments is not other than the consciousness.

**Memory as the Lord's power: how the "I" holds time together**

The jñānādhikāra has established knowledge; now it takes up memory. And here Abhinavagupta makes a
startling claim. The ordinary view — the view of the schools — is that memory is only the revival of an
impression after the experience is gone. When the experience is destroyed, a mere trace remains, and
memory is the stirring of that trace. But Abhinavagupta rejects this. Memory, he insists, is itself a
*knowledge*; and far from being a pale echo of experience, it is the **Lord's own power** — the
un-broken manifestation by which the past and the present are held together in the single "I."

Consider what memory actually does. It brings the previously-experienced object back before the mind;
the object appears, again, in the knower. If memory were only an impression's revival, this would be
inexplicable — for how could a mere trace present an object? The truth is that memory is the un-broken
manifestation of the experienced object: the experience and its object are carried forward into the
memory as one. In memory, the experience does not stand apart as a separate object; it is the very act
of knowing that returns. Even the yogin's knowledge of another, Abhinavagupta notes, does not appear as
a detached object — it is the one awareness continuing. The separation that memory seems to make between
the past cognition and the present one is only a construction (kālpanika), not a real division. And
ultimately, the remembered, the memory, and the rememberer — and by the same token the seen, the seeing,
and the seer — all rest in the one consciousness-essence.

Now the "I" itself. The "aham" shines in two directions at once. As "the seer of the blue" it is turned
inward; but the same "I, thus" is also turned outward toward the blue. The experience is the outward-
facing blue-knowledge. And here is the freedom: by the freedom of the awareness, one first construes,
within, "I would see the blue," and then the blue appears without. The inner construing precedes the
outer manifestation, as the seed precedes the sprout. So the object, tinted by its place and its time,
enters the knower and the experience together; and in the memory "I saw the blue then," the three — the
I, the blue, the then — appear entered into that one act.

This is the key to time itself. When we say "the jar stands, will stand, stood," what makes this
possible is the un-brokenness of the manifestation — the awareness that holds the jar's appearances
together across the moments. The experience is the gate through which time is entered. As long as the
awareness is not touched by time, there is no time-dealing at all; but when it manifests the jar in its
past, present, and future, time appears. And the one who says "I" across all of this is the same — the
one self, who saw, who remembers, who will see. Memory is the thread by which the "I" holds time
together, and it is, in the end, the Lord's own power shining as the un-broken awareness.

**The self-luminous cognition: how memory reaches the past, and the yogin reaches the other**

Two puzzles press on the account of memory. The first is the pastness of the past. We remember what
happened yesterday — but how, if the manifestation of consciousness has no touch of time at all? The
answer is that the pastness is not a real quality of the object; it is the *being-previously-manifested*.
The one light, contracting under the limiting conditions of place and time — "yesterday, thirsty, with
that friend, I saw this jar un-ripe" — appears as the past. The manifestation is cut by these upādhis;
and what we call the māyā-word, the realm of ordinary experience, is precisely this contraction of the
light by the conditions. The memory is the re-apprehension of what was previously manifested; and the
cognition of the object, so cut by the past experience, is itself a fresh act of experience. There is
nothing ghostly in memory: it is the one light, narrowed to a past moment, shining again.

The second puzzle is the yogin's perception of another's mind. The yogin is the one who has attained
unity with the supreme knower; for him, all objects are un-cut by time, present in his own self as "I"
or as "I-this." How, then, does one particular appearance arise for him, and with its past-time-
specificity? Here Abhinavagupta gives the key: time is the order of appearing and not-appearing. The
body, flashing and fading moment by moment, is what gives the endless difference of time. Those who
take the body as the knower are bound in the chain of time, and can never see past or future. But the
yogin, by the teaching and the sustained meditation, thins the body — and then the other's cognition
shines in its own place.

And this leads to the deepest point: the nature of cognition itself. The cognition is
self-cognition (svasaṃvitti). Its own nature — that which never deviates, the marker neither over- nor
under-pervading — is to be self-luminous, the own-awareness that distinguishes it utterly from the
inert. The jar is not self-aware; it is only what it is. But cognition, in its very being, is aware of
itself. And precisely because it is self-cognition, it is also free to manifest the *other*: the same
luminous awareness that knows itself can, in its freedom, shine upon another's cognition. The inert
cannot do this; only the self-luminous awareness can. So the yogin's knowledge of another is nothing
other than the other's own-cognition, self-luminous, which the yogin — by the purity and the un-opposed
spreading of his own cognition — comes to know.

The upshot is a single, elegant thesis. Cognition is self-cognition: it is the own-awareness that is
the very nature of consciousness, distinguishing it from the inert. And because it is self-cognition, it
is also other-manifesting — it can reach the past in memory, and reach the other in the yogin's
perception. Memory and clairvoyance are not exceptions to the nature of cognition; they are the
overflow of the one self-luminous awareness, which, being aware of itself, is free to be aware of all.

**The self-luminous cognition is never the object of another**

We have seen that the yogin, by the purity and the un-opposed spreading of his cognition, knows
another's cognition. But this draws a sharp objection from the epistemologist. "Even granting that," he
says, "a cognition can never be the *object* of another cognition. For how can one awareness be known
by a second? The two would have to stand in the relation of object and holder — and between two
cognitions no such relation is possible."

Abhinavagupta takes this seriously and analyzes what "being an object" really means. A thing is an
object of a cognition when the awareness *assimilates its form* — when it takes on the form of the
thing, as the blue-awareness takes on the blue. This assimilation is the sārūpya, the conformity of the
cognition to its object. And it requires that the object be *both* like and unlike the cognition: in
total identity the thing would be the cognition itself, and in total difference there would be nothing
to assimilate. Now here is the crux. A cognition has no such difference from another cognition. The
difference of place, time, and form is absent between two awarenesses; the difference that comes from
the object (the blue) is not the param-essence of the cognition; and though the object-part — the blue
— or the intent-part — the passion — can be an object by a separate manifestation, the *awareness-part*
itself can never be an object at all. An awareness cannot be spread before itself as a thing to be
grasped.

Abhinavagupta makes this vivid with two mirrors. Two mirrors can reflect one another, each bearing the
other's image — because their forms, being of place and time, are genuinely distinct. But two
cognitions are not like that. Their form is not the place-time form of things; it is the self-luminous
awareness, which has nothing in it to be set over against another awareness. So the object-holder
relation between two cognitions is impossible: there is no perception of any real difference between
them (this is the epistemologist's own anupalabdhi, turned against him).

And what of māyā — does it not cover the awareness and make it an object? No. Māyā does not really
cover the awareness's own form, any more than a covering hides the burning power of the fire; and even
what we call a covering is, in truth, the producing of a form distinct from the prior state. The
awareness is not hidden by the world; it is the world that appears in the awareness.

The upshot is decisive. The cognition is self-luminous. It is never made the object of another
cognition — because to be an object is to be assimilated by an awareness, and one awareness cannot
assimilate another without the real difference that awarenesses lack. The knower, in other words, is
fundamentally *conscious* — the ajaḍa, the not-inert — a self-luminous presence that is never itself
turned into a thing. This is the establishment of the conscious knower, with which the vimarśa on
memory, and the whole Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi, comes to its close.

**The knowledge-power: manifestation as the very form of things**

We have examined memory and the construction. But both presuppose something deeper — the
knowledge-power (jñānaśakti), the capacity by which anything at all is known. And here Abhinavagupta
makes the central claim of this vimarśa: **the manifestation is the very form of the objects.** The
things of the world are not hidden realities that a light shines upon from outside; their being *is*
their being-manifested. To know a thing is not to touch something beyond the light; it is to be the
light in which that thing appears.

Consider the present beings. As they manifest, they manifest "as the outer-self" — the inner
standing-alone of consciousness, pouring itself out as the external world. The jar before you is not a
thing outside that your mind then copies; it is the inner light, standing as the outer form. Memory and
the construction, for their part, do not present a common object as something separate and distinct; and
even in perception, the object does not exceed the experience that reveals it. The thing is not more
than its being-manifested.

Now the Vijñānavādin, the Buddhist idealist, agrees that the object is not outside — but he draws the
wrong conclusion. He concludes that there is no object at all, only the inner cognition with its blue
form. Abhinavagupta replies that this does not follow. The cognition's inner blue-form is a
*reflection*; and a reflection expects a ground that it reflects — as a mirror-image expects the thing
before the mirror. So the inner blue-form, being a reflection, points to an identical ground that
produces it. This is the inference of the object: not as a thing hidden beyond all experience, but as
the ground whose reflection the blue-form is. Even as the sense-organ is inferred from the perception
it causes, so the object is inferred as the cause of its manifestation. The object is real — but its
reality is to be the ground of the manifestation, not a bare thing beyond it.

And this is the deep point. The objects necessarily inhere in the consciousness-self, by the very
re-recollection (parāmarśa) through which they are known. And the essence of the manifestation — the
knowledge-power — is the reflexive-awareness (vimarśa). The light is not a passive mirror; it is the
self-aware light that, in knowing the object, knows itself. The known is not something set over against
the knower; the knowledge-re-recollection is itself the known, the pure, never abandoning the
knower-being. Even in the un-constructed perception, the life is the reflexive-awareness. So the
knowledge-power is not the capacity to reach some hidden thing; it is the self-luminous, self-aware
manifestation that is the very being of the world.

The upshot: the jñānaśakti is the manifestation that constitutes the objects. The world is not lit
from without; it is the light. The object is not a fiction, nor a thing beyond the light, but the ground
that the manifestation reflects; and the essence of that manifestation is the reflexive-awareness —
the light that knows itself in knowing all. This is the knowledge-power, the first and deepest of the
powers of consciousness.

**How the external object is inferred and confirmed**

The Vijñānavādin grants that the cognition is self-luminous, but he presses on its inner form. "The
cognition's blue-form," he says, "is a reflection (pratibimba); and a reflection demands a ground that
produces it (the arpaka). So the external object is inferred." But then the classic objection follows:
how can you infer an external object that is never perceived? An inference rests on a pervasion grasped
in perception — and the external is never perceived at all.

Abhinavagupta answers with the sense-organ analogy. The sense-organ itself is never perceived — yet we
infer it as the cause of the perceptions it produces. The eye is inferred from the seeing, not seen.
So too the external object: though never perceived as an object, it is inferred as the cause of its
cognition. And the mechanism is the sārūpya, the conformity: the inner blue-form, with all its
place-and-time variety, un-lost, points to its ground — the object similar to it. The determination "I
see this object" arises from this conformity, and it is not a bare error, like the shell-silver in the
grasped shell.

For here is the crucial point, and Abhinavagupta states it boldly: even this determination, though it
begins as error — the drawing of the inner form outward — is, by its bond to the thing, a *valid means*.
As the rule has it, "even the error, being a relation, is a pramā." The determination, by the strength
of the seeing, takes the form "I see" and enlists the perception as the object's helper — as a minister
moves a king who has been won over. So the external object, thus determined and confirmed, is
perceived (pratyakṣa-gṛhīta).

And what, then, is the inference's own work? It is the sasaṃvāda — the agreement. The inference
establishes that the root-cause, the ground of the forms (the arpaka), is the object similar to the
form. This is its operation: not to create the object, but to confirm that the ground of the cognition's
form is the thing, the similar thing, which the determination had already perceived.

And if the inference were to work the other way — to refute the external, as the reasoning from
momentariness refutes stability — then the whole determination of the external would be uprooted, and
the practical dealings of the world would fail. If it did not determine at all, the dealing would
likewise fail. So the external object, perceived and confirmed by the agreement, stands: it is real, and
the cognition of it, with the perception as its helper and the inference as its confirmation, is a
valid means.

The upshot is a balanced realism. The object is not a bare thing hidden beyond all cognition; it is the
ground of the cognition's form, inferred like the sense-organ and confirmed by the agreement. The
determination "I see the jar" is not a fiction — it is a valid means, because it is bound to the thing
and confirmed by the agreement. The external object is real, and the way we know it — perception and
inference together — is sound.

**You cannot infer another's mind — and you do not need the external object**

The Buddhist hopes to escape by inferring *another's* mind. He thinks: from Maitra's speech, from his
uttered words and gestures, one can infer what is going on in his mind — the other stream. Abhinavagupta
shows this inference cannot work, and he does it with a precise analogy.

Suppose you want to infer the fire *in the sandalwood* from the smoke. If you set aside the
sandalwood's fragrance — the very thing that marks this smoke as coming from sandalwood — then you
establish only fire in general, not the sandalwood-fire. The distinction must be accepted; without it
the desired conclusion is not reached. But to infer another's mind, you would need exactly such a
further distinction — the "being-gone-to-the-other," the fact that this utterance belongs to Maitra and
not to you. And that distinction cannot be inferred from the mere utterance. The utterance could belong
to anything; nothing in it, by itself, says "this is Maitra's intent, this is another's mind."

And the "being-gone-to-the-other," Abhinavagupta argues, is not like the sandalwood-fragrance, a
further distinguishing mark resting apart from the thing. It is a different kind of thing entirely. To
press the point, he notes that if every additional feature were a "further distinction," then "cow" and
"speckled" would both be separate things, and the statement "the cow is the speckled" would fail. But
that statement holds; so a real further-distinction is something that rests apart from the thing, and
the "being-gone-to-the-other" does not rest apart from the mere utterance in the way that would make it
inferable.

Moreover — and this is the decisive point — only the *aimed* action (samīhitā) is the wish's effect.
A wish produces the action it intends, not a mere utterance or gesture that could be aimed at anything.
So from Maitra's mere utterance one cannot infer his wish, since the utterance does not reveal which
aim it serves. If the mere utterance sufficed, then even the most grotesque case — a piśāca-like action
in someone's appearing — would have to be established as his intent, which is absurd.

So the other-stream cannot be inferred; the mere appearances do not reach another's mind. And this
paves the way for kārikā 6: the appearances alone suffice for the dealings of the world. We do not need
a hidden external object behind the appearances to explain our dealing with the jar, the fire, the
person. The appearance — the ābhāsa — is enough. And from this follows the refutation of the external
object: whether it is posited as a whole (the avayavin of the Nyāya) or as atoms (the paramāṇu of the
Vaibhāṣika), the external thing is needless. Only the appearance is real, and it is the appearance that
serves our object-action (arthakriyā). The world of our dealing is the world of the appearances — and
these, being the manifestation of consciousness, are real.

**The Lord creates from within, like a yogin**

The external object has been demolished. The whole (avayavin) cannot stand: a jar has shadow on one
side and sun on the other, its middle covered and its sides uncovered — so the one whole that was to
bear all these contradictory states is impossible. And the atom (paramāṇu) fares no better: the middle
atom, being part-less, cannot have two sides, one sun-lit and one shaded; the two-part atom collapses
back into the whole it was meant to replace; and the parts run on to infinity. Whether the Buddhist
posits a whole or atoms, the external thing has no valid means behind it. It cannot be established.

But then the objector asks a fair question: "You yourself established the external by the variety of
the appearance-order, as its cause. So how is it un-established now?" And this is where Abhinavagupta
turns from destruction to construction. The external is not needed, because the Lord manifests the
whole world from within himself, by his own will, without any external material cause — exactly as a
yogin does.

Consider what has been granted on all sides. The consciousness-form is the locus in which objects are
established; and by its power of synthesis it is one. Its lordship — its very God-ness — is the freedom
to join and separate the appearances. And the objects are, in their being, the manifestation of this
consciousness. So the whole world is, from the first, *within* the consciousness — the inner-containing-
world-form. And with this freedom there must be the will: the un-thwarted will, whose very nature is
freedom. And that the will creates — without any external cause — is already seen in the dream. In the
dream, the jar appears, and the whole clay-wheel-stick-lineage of causes is absent. The dream proves
that the consciousness alone can create an object-mass, by its will, without a material cause.

The objection: "then the jar is unreal." Let it be so, Abhinavagupta answers — and still the point
holds. For the yogin creates an army, a city, by the mere will. If someone says "the atoms are joined by
the will, as the material cause," then if the whole known cause-complement (the clay, the wheel, the
helpers) were accepted, the yogin would be just a potter. But when he transcends the known — creates
with even a straw — the dream and the construction show that the consciousness's power to bring about
the being-appearance needs no external cause at all. As the verse has it: "no other cause of the
dream's object-variety is seen than your manifestation-power; being seen to have that power, it alone
is the one cause of the whole world's manifestation."

so how much more the pure consciousness-tattva, which everywhere is the creator. The God, the
consciousness-self, manifests the whole object-mass from within himself, by his will, like a yogin,
without any external material cause. This is the īśvarādvaya — the non-dual lordship. The world is not
made from a stuff outside the Lord; it is his own inner being, manifested outward by his will. And this
is why the external object was never needed: not because the world is unreal, but because its reality

**The light that knows itself: the heart of the doctrine**

Here, in the deepest part of the vimarśa on the knowledge-power, Abhinavagupta states the heart of the
whole teaching. The manifestation (prakāśa) is not a passive, inert light. Its very nature is the
*reflexive-awareness* (vimarśa) — the light's own grasp of itself. Without the vimarśa, the
manifestation would be like crystal: it would show the world, but it would not know that it showed it;
it would be inert. What makes the light *light* — what makes it consciousness and not a thing — is that
it is aware of itself in the very act of manifesting.

Consider the very first surge of knowing. In the inner speech, the middle-self, before the mind has
split the knower from the known — in the paśyantī, the seeing, the first stirring of the will — the
knower and the known are not yet two, not even by their common form; no distinction has yet flashed.
And this, Abhinavagupta says, shines by itself. It is the pure reflexive-awareness before any division.

The proof that this is so is drawn from the swiftest of our acts. In quick reading, in rapid motion,
in hurried speech, we go from line to line, from place to place, abandoning some things and seizing
others — all without pausing to reflect. Yet these abandonments and attainments are, as we see, always
preceded by a re-reflection (parāmarśa). They infer their cause, the re-reflection. And that
re-reflection cannot be only by the difference of knower and known — for then the very swiftness of the
act would fail, tangled in the lineage of speech, mind, motion, convention, memory. The swift act shows
that the knower and the known, the abandoning and the attaining, are not two separate things: they are
one act of the self-aware consciousness. What is, and is not separate, must be non-separate — there is
no third class to hold them apart.

And this is the will — the first surge, the first "tuṭi" (the bursting). As the Śivadṛṣṭi says: when
the consciousness-dharma, in its splendor and joy, unfolds into the varied creation, and becomes the
un-lidded awareness — that is the will's first surge. And she is seen in the sudden moments: in the
heart, at the time of remembering an effect, at the moment of rapture or emotion, at the sight of the
beloved, at the un-reflected glance, at the very emission of the utterance, in the reading and the
running. In all these occasions, the all-power-liveliness of the consciousness flashes. It is the
reflexive-awareness, the self-grasping of the light, seen most clearly where the mind does not pause to
divide.

So the reflexive-awareness is not a thing, not an added quality — it is the manifestation's own nature.
The light that shines is the light that knows itself; and this self-knowing is the parā-vāk, the
supreme speech, from which all the lower levels of speech (the madhyamā, the vaikharī) descend. It is
the Lord's freedom (svātantrya) and his lordship (aiśvarya). This is what Abhinavagupta will draw out
in the next kārikās — that consciousness is at once the awareness, its action, and its agency (kārikā
12), and that this reflexive-awareness, the parā-vāk, arising by its own savor, is the supreme freedom
of the supreme self (kārikā 13). The heart of the doctrine is here: the light knows itself, and that
self-knowing is the Lord.

**The powers of the Lord are his reflexive-awareness**

The reflexive-awareness is the heart of the doctrine. Now Abhinavagupta must show what this means for
the powers — and, first, what it does *not* mean. The grammarian would make speech, the paśyantī, a
separate supreme principle. But speech and the mind, Abhinavagupta insists, are only the operation of

power is the varied, the distinct-and-non-distinct; he is the great form of the fifth mantra, the
reflexive-awareness that is the manifestation-form. But the māyīya phonemes — the words we actually
speak — are like the jar; the knowledge that raises them (the paśyantī-madhyamā) is like another
cognition; and the speech-organ is like the hand, placed in the side of māyā. None of these is the
supreme. They are of the object-cognition-organ form.

And yet — and this is the delicate point — where the word does its work, where it succeeds in its own
part of the action, that success is not its own: it is made by the touch of the supreme power. As the
teaching says, "from the self-power-touch…" the things become givers of the fruit of all desires. The
power that makes the word effective is the reflexive-awareness of the Lord, flowing through it. What
is contracted by time, place, form, and action is not the param — like the jar. And the param-ness is
fullness (pūrṇatva); its opposite, the contraction, is what the experience refutes. The paśu-form — the
word, the cognition, the organ — is contracted; the param is the full, which the vimarśa is.

And this leads to the positive account of the powers. The throbbing (sphurattā) — the very pulsing of
the manifestation — is the great being (mahāsattā), undivided by place and time, the heart of the
param-Lord (kārikā 14). It is the same as the spanda, the wave (ūrmi), the eternal being. And the
powers by which the Lord acts — the making of the known (jñeyīkaraṇa), the constructing and dealing
with himself (k15–16) — these are all the reflexive-awareness. The division of the "I"-awareness and
the "this"-awareness (ahantā/idantā) is no ground for the self's otherness (k17): the self remains one
in both. And the powers of cognition, of conception, of determination (jñāna, saṃkalpa, adhyavasāya)

Lord's power-touch. And the vimarśa is present everywhere — in the sudden surge, in the direct
manifestation, in the determination — because it is the very nature of the light, the heart of the
param-Lord.

**Memory's seed and the "this jar" are the reflexive-awareness**

The reflexive-awareness is the source of the powers. Now Abhinavagupta shows that even the *impression*
— the seed of memory — is nothing without it. How does a memory get laid down, and how does it awaken?
The schools would say: the experience lays a trace, and the later seeing of something like it awakens
the trace. But Abhinavagupta presses: what makes the experience strong enough to lay the seed? It is
the resting of the experience in the reflexive-awareness — the moment in which the experience is aware
of itself, "I, thus, shine." Without that self-awareness, the experience would be an inert flash; it
could not lay a seed, nor could it be awakened. The non-construction, the bare sensory flash, cannot do
it.

The Bhaṭṭa had said the strength of the experience is what lays the seed. But even this strength,
Abhinavagupta replies, is the resting in the knower — the reflexive-awareness. If the light's
manifestation, its being-strong, is not admitted, then nothing at all would lay a seed; and the
not-strong would have to be the awakener too, making the whole "strong" distinction meaningless. The
point is driven home with the smoke-and-fire example. "Fire-ness itself is the smoke-cause-ness" — we
see this in the fire. If the mere impression, without the vimarśa, laid the memory, then even the
coconut-island dweller, who has never seen smoke, would remember fire from smoke. But he does not.
Without the vimarśa-form cause, the impression is neither laid nor awakened — just as the smoke does
not awaken the fire-memory in one who never knew fire.

And this is the deeper point: the very act by which we take the world — the determination
(adhyavasāya) — is itself the reflexive-awareness. When we say "this jar," the determination "this
jar" is not a mere name-and-form, a word pasted onto a thing. It is, Abhinavagupta declares in kārikā
20, *beyond* name and form: it is the param-Lord's power, manifesting like the self, not by the
this-ness. The "this" of the jar is not something the jar has from outside; it is the Lord's own
reflexive-awareness, shining through the act of determination. The vācya-vācaka (the signified and the
signifier), the sphoṭa — all these analyses fail, because the "this-ness" they try to locate in the
word or the thing is really the self's own manifestation.

So memory and determination are both the reflexive-awareness. The impression is laid and awakened only
by the vimarśa; and the determination "this jar," far from being a word pasted on a thing, is the
param-Lord's power manifesting like the self. The vimarśa is not one power among others; it is the
very form of the light, present in the memory's seed, in the determination's "this," and in every act
by which the self knows and takes its world.

**The word is self-luminous, and the order is only in the objects**

We have said that the reflexive-awareness is the very nature of the manifestation. Now the vimarśa on
the knowledge-power closes by drawing out two consequences — one about words, one about order.

First, the word. When we say "this jar," the "this" seems to be a thing that the word "jar" is pasted
onto. But Abhinavagupta shows this is a mistake. The "jar"-word, in the determination, does not stand
apart as a free thing that the "this" points at; it is superimposed on the meaning, and the
"this"-re-recollection is made with the non-difference. If the word were not superimposed, it would be
recalled as a free-standing sound — "from this fire, ḍhak" — not as the speaker of a meaning. The
conventional word (like the "cloth"-word after the convention) does not shine by a bare experience, as
a quality like "white" does; it shines by being superimposed on the meaning. So the relation of word and
meaning is not a distinction of two things but a superimposition (adhyāsa).

And this brings us to the word's own nature. If the manifested were not re-recollected, its being-
manifested itself would be impossible. As the external blue, being manifested, is re-recollected as
"blue," so the word — which is itself a manifestation — necessarily has the reflexive-awareness. There
is no further word, general or specific, by which it would be recalled as the blue-speaker; and to call
it by another similar word would run into the infinite regress, destroying the blue-re-recollection and
so the blue-manifestation itself. Hence the own-form-re-recollection is the very nature of the meaning.
And because the "blue"-word is the re-collector, its being able to re-collect itself and the other is
its self-luminousness (svaprakāśatva).

The lamp makes this clear. The lamp shines, revealing the objects and itself — not because it bears the
covering shadow, but because its being-shining is its own. The same is true of the word and of the
manifestation: by the same act of shining, it reveals the object and reveals itself. The
reflexive-awareness-kindling is both the fruit-ground and the seed-ground of the manifestation. The
cognition, shining by itself, by that very shining makes the object shine — it is clearly
self-and-other-manifesting. So the lamp is self-and-other-light; the word is self-and-other-
re-recollection.

Second, the order. We see cognition, memory, determination following one another, ordered in time. But
this order, kārikā 21 declares, is only by the place-and-time of the *different cognized* objects. The
cognition of the blue, then the memory of it, then the determination — these seem to be a sequence. But
in themselves, the reflexive-awareness-resting cognitions are one and order-less (akrama). The order
belongs to the objects, to the places and times that the cognized things carry; the awareness that
knows them all is one, without sequence, resting in itself. Just as the Lord is free of order though he
shows order, so the single reflexive-awareness is order-less, appearing ordered only through the
objects' place-and-time.

With this, the jñānaśakti vimarśa — the reflexive-awareness of the knowledge-power — comes to its
close. The word is self-luminous, the manifestation reveals itself and the other, and the order of our
cognitions is only in the objects, while the awareness itself is one and order-less. The knowledge-power
is, in the end, the single self-luminous reflexive-awareness, free of order, revealing itself and the
world.

**The "I" is not a construction**

We have established knowledge and memory. Now Abhinavagupta takes up the third power — the apohana, the
removal — that serves both. And at its heart lies a question that threatens the whole doctrine. The
reflexive-awareness, we have said, is the manifestation's own nature. But the reflexive-awareness is
word-joined; and the word-joined, it might seem, is a construction (vikalpa). If so, then the Lord's own
self-awareness would be a construction — which cannot be. The construction is of the māyā-form, the
saṃsāric; how could it be in the Lord?

Kārikā 1 answers this, and its answer is precise. The "I"-recollection (ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa) — even
though it has the word as its body — is *not* a construction. It is the fit, the two-throwing, the
determination.

Consider what the pure "I"-recollection is. It is the self-grasp of the manifestation free of the
contraction by the body and the rest — the grasp of the self-nature, resting in the freedom, supreme,
foundational: the "I." This, Abhinavagupta insists, is not a construction. And to see why, we must ask
what a construction actually is. The construction (vikalpa, the vivida-kalpanā) is of three kinds: it
joins what is distinct (as one joins molasses, curd, and pepper into a compound); it constructs the one
in many ways; or it splits off a doubted, other form. All three are operations of division and joining,
of this-and-that.

But the "I"-recollection is none of these. It does not join a distinct "this" to a distinct "I"; it is
the single self-grasp, resting in itself. It does not construct the one into many; it is the one.
It does not split off a doubted other; it is the un-doubted foundation. The "I" is not built up out of
parts, nor split out of a doubt — it is the pure self-awareness that underlies every construction, the
very thing that makes construction possible, without itself being one.

This is the apohanaśakti at its root. The removal — the power by which the self excludes what is not
itself — is not a construction that the self performs upon itself; it is the self's own grasp, the pure
"I" that, in knowing itself, is the foundation of all the word-joined, constructed dealings of the
world. And this pure "I"-recollection, resting in the freedom, is the Lord's self-awareness — not a
māyā-form construction, but the very nature of the manifestation, the self-grasp that is the Lord.
The apohana, the removal, is not a cutting off; it is the self's own luminous grasp, the "I" that is
one, un-divided, and free.
