**The Lord descends through the states, and deals with the world**

The consciousness does not remain aloof. It descends, step by step, into the forms of the world — and
this descent is the story of the bound knower. Abhinavagupta traces it through the states. The
consciousness, entering the known-form, takes up the void, the breath, the intellect, the body, in
order. Even space, the most permissive of forms, is not wholly inert; the wind, with its power of
movement, less so; the light, with its form and brilliance, still less; the water, which receives what
enters it; and finally the coarse, dense earth, the most inert of all. And with each descent, the
self-conceit sinks further — as the elephant sinks into the mud-bank — until the consciousness comes to
identify itself with the coarse body. For the world, the first of these is the breath (prāṇa): the
touch-form, the moving, that takes up the void-following and, with the fire-connection, presides over
the rest. The consciousness-tattva is what presides over the prāṇa, which presides over the intellect,
the puryaṣṭaka (the inner city), and the body.

So the Lord, the consciousness-form, presides over the body *through* the prāṇa and the puryaṣṭaka —
not directly, by a bare experience, but as the inner light that animates them. As the Gītā says, "whatever
body the Lord attains, and whatever he departs, taking these, he goes, as the wind takes the fragrances
from the flower-bed." The īśvara, the consciousness-form, goes from body to body through the
prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka, as the wind carries the scents. And the Spandakārikā's "with the inner wheel" is
this same prāṇa, by which the organ-group obtains its proceeding, standing, and withdrawal.

And because the consciousness, through the prāṇa, presides over the states, the enjoyment continues even
after the body's death. As in the dream — the state immersed in sleep, the delusion — the
prāṇa-embraced puryaṣṭaka, being the same, passes on, and the enjoyment in the other world, by the
presiding over another body, is not impossible. The yogins are seen, remaining in their own body and
their own house, to be elsewhere — proving the consciousness's power to preside beyond the present body.

This leads to the kārikās. The construction (vikalpa, kārikā 6) is the joining of the "this" from the
prior appearance, by the impression — it rests in the different manifestations, and it is a
construction. But the *continuity* (anusandhāna) — the self that runs through the body, mind, breath,
through all the states, from life to life — is not a construction; it is the one consciousness,
un-divided. And in the dealing (kārikā 7), the Lord, entering the body, manifests the inner
object-mass without, by the will. The world we deal with is the Lord's own inner mass, manifested
outward by his will, through the very states through which he descends.

And this is the kṛtyapañcaka — the fivefold work. The Lord creates, causes to stand, withdraws,
conceals, and graces — and all five are his dealing, his manifestation of the inner mass through the
states. The consciousness that descends through the void, the breath, the intellect, and the body is
the same Lord who creates and deals with the whole world. The bound knower's descent is the Lord's
descent; the dealing is the Lord's dealing; and the fivefold work is the Lord's own manifestation,
through the prāṇa and the puryaṣṭaka, of the inner world without.

**The inner appearance stands firm — for every living one**

The ṣaṣṭho vimarśa, on the power of removal, comes to its close; and its final claim is one of
unfailing constancy. The inner appearance — the self-grasp, the reflexive-awareness — stands firm in
memory, in construction, and in cognition alike (kārikā 8). It is not something that flickers in and
out, present in cognition and absent in memory. It is the one light that runs through them all. In the
cognition whose form is the external manifestation, this inner appearance — the prior-experience-form —
is innate (kārikā 9); and it stands, too, in memory and the rest. In the freely-wandering construction,
the inner appearance is innate indeed (kārikā 10): the construction may wander at will, forming this or
that shape, but the self-grasp that shapes it is always there, in the mind's range. And hence — from the
manifestation of the uplifting as wished — knowledge and action are clear, established for every living
one (kārikā 11).

And this constancy extends even to the freed. Even in liberation, the freed souls (muktāṇava) are
distinct — yet their manifestation, by the śiva-ness, is the un-broken all-knowing. The three-time
manifestation may be established in the māyīya knower, but it does not fail to flash for them either,
from their all-knowing. And the mantreśvaras — even in liberation, by the exhaustion of their authority,
in the place of the other — by the word-obtaining (the dīkṣā, the vow, the japa, the tapas, the
concentration, the conduct), transmigrating, are all-knowing; the knower-ness is not de-valued. The
animal-atoms are distinct only in their animal-ness, generally. The categories, the worlds, the
elements, the kalā, the mantra, the word, the phoneme — the jars and the rest, with respect to their
own class, are not utterly unprecedented.

The objection "how, in the dealing-time, is the creation?" is met. The creation is by the unity — at
that time, per-knower, the jar-appearance and the body-appearance are distinct, but the consciousness-
self alone [creates them]; and the knower-distinction is not destroyed, for it stands in the
prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka and the like. And the appearance is the cognition: the jar-form appearance, though
known, is of the knower-operation-form, of the knower-standing-ness — it is the cognition itself. The
final objection — "then by the knower's will, per-moment the creation and withdrawal of objects and
knowers — how does the maheśvara shine?" — is answered: the order-word's pure-form-sequence is not the
whole; the maheśvara, the Lord, is the one who shines through it all.

So the vimarśa closes with the constancy of the self-grasp. It is innate in memory, in cognition, in
construction; it stands firm for the bound and for the freed, for the animal-atom and the mantreśvara;
and from its manifestation — the uplifting as wished — knowledge and action are clear for every living
one. The inner appearance, the reflexive-awareness, never fails: it is the very nature of the light,
and it is what makes every living one a knower and a doer. The apohanaśaktivimarśa — the reflexion on
the power of removal — here comes to its close.

**The one support of all the powers**

The powers — knowledge, memory, removal — have been established. But a power does not float free; it
needs a support (āśraya). And the question now is: what supports the powers? The ordinary answer would
make the support inert, like the fire's relation to its powers of burning, cooking, and sweating. But
Abhinavagupta insists this is wrong. The support of the powers is the maheśvara — the Lord — and his
essence is not to be a thing that happens to have powers, but to be the very freedom of joining,
separating, resting, concealing, and manifesting. He is not the inert base that the powers sit upon;
he is the free act in which the powers are his own unfolding.

The whole saptamo vimarśa is devoted to proving that this one support exists and that it is the Lord.
The plan is laid out: one verse states the support's own form; two prove it by the presence-and-absence
(anvaya-vyatireka) — in the one support the dealing of the world is fit, without it, not; one states
the dealing (the cognition-aggregation, resting in the knower, of the cause-effect form); one the
memory (the knower-rest); eight the whole dealing (the true-and-false division); and one the conclusion.

And the first verse gives the support's own form in a striking image: the pratibhā. The pratibhā is the
flashing — the light that runs through the ordered word-objects, through all the varied things we name
and know. It is seasoned (rūṣitā) with their order, touched by it. But the flashing itself is not
ordered. Its support — that in which the flashing flashes, the one who knows the order without being
caught in it — is the order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower. And that knower, Abhinavagupta
declares, is the great Lord (maheśvara).

So the first word of the vimarśa is this: the flashing world, with all its order and variety, is the
manifestation of a knower who is not ordered, who is not caught in the variety, who is the infinite
consciousness. The ordered word-objects flash in the order-less light. And this is not an inert light,
but the free Lord — the one whose very being is the freedom to join and separate, to conceal and to
manifest. He is the support of all the powers: the powers are his freedom, and he is their support, the
one, order-less, infinite consciousness, the great Lord.

**The valid means is the knower's own operation**

The saptamo vimarśa is establishing the one support of the powers. And its deepest point is that the
valid means (pramāṇa) is not a separate instrument standing over against the knower. It is the
knower's own operation (pramātṛ-vyāpāra) — the act by which the many cognitions are gathered into the
one knower. The five objects of perception and non-perception, thrown into the one consciousness-ocean,
are joined by the freedom-wave, becoming mutually dependent (jar and cloth, as it were); they shine
with their distinct appearances and are re-reflected. The one appearance, made by the
manifestation-operation of the five, is the cause-and-effect appearance; and the re-recollection is
the knower's operation. This — the joining — is the whole logic of the valid means. Without it, even
the pramāṇas are useless. As the Mukuta-saṃhitā says, the consciousness-operation alone is the one
reason, established everywhere, in enjoyment or in liberation. The joiner alone is the means.

Now the objection presses on memory. "By perception and non-perception," the objector says, "what was
made is to be unified; this much is the acceptance of the knower. But what is this? In the
unification, the memory alone is engaged." And Abhinavagupta answers with kārikā 5: in memory, that
very self-consciousness is the valid means in the self's birth; in the prior-experience-being, it is
the proof — that alone, not another.

Consider what happens when we remember. The memory seems to bring back a prior object. But it does not
bring a *new* thing, a fresh appearance supplied by the memory-time — for memory is of the
grasped-grasping nature; it re-grasps what was already grasped. What shines in the memory is the prior
experience itself. And it does not now stand as a separate known object — for if it did, we would have
the cognition of a known cognition (jñātajñāna), which is not memory at all; and no cognition is
known-by-another (as we have shown at length). So, if the prior experience were a separate
self-luminous thing, we would have two unconnected experiences, not a memory. The only way the memory
is possible is that, at the memory-time, the prior experience itself — being the inner self-consciousness
— is what shines. The memory is the prior experience, self-conscious, remembered.

And this is the point. The memory is not a second cognition standing over against a first; it is the
same self-consciousness, the same knower, continuing. The valid means in memory — and in every
cognition — is the self-consciousness of the one knower. It is the knower's own operation, the act by
which he knows and re-knows himself. And this is why the one knower is the support of all the powers:
knowledge, memory, and removal are all his own self-conscious operation. The valid means is not a thing
the knower uses; it is the knower himself, the one who remembers, the same self-consciousness in the
self's birth and in the memory — that alone, not another.

**The omniscient knows all — and his non-perception establishes**

The saptamo vimarśa, on the one support of the powers, closes with the figure of the omniscient — the
supreme knower who is the support. And the question that tests him is the goblin, the piśāca. Suppose
there is a piśāca in the dark interval. We do not see it; but the atoms of form and the rest are there,
unseen by us, seen by the omniscient. The piśāca's atoms, for the omniscient, are no different from the
atoms of the darkness and the other beings — he sees them all. If the piśāca is truly absent, then where
it might have stood, the omniscient sees only the atoms of light (āloka), and these — being seen — are
the very ground of his dealing "there is no piśāca here."

But the objector presses: "seeing all the other objects, how does the omniscient deny a *distinct*
piśāca?" The answer is subtle. Whatever is, the omniscient sees it; so if, in that place, he does not
see the piśāca, then it is not there. Everything in that place is the piśāca-included thing — the whole
known together — and its being or not-being is decided by his seeing. The distinct-piśāca's-absence is
established by the omniscient's whole, un-broken perception, not by any tracing of the interval's
atoms.

And why is this not so for us? Because we see only the limited (arvāk). For one who sees the limited,
there is no such un-broken knowledge: his non-perception of the piśāca is only the limited — the
grasped-as-if-un-grasped — not the established non-being. There is no cause, in his limited seeing, to
remove the conceiving of the distinct thing in that place. The omniscient's non-perception, by contrast,
establishes; the limited seer's does not.

The final objection: "if the piśāca's non-negatability is caused by its invisibility, then the jar's
negatability should be caused by its visibility." But this fails: every negation, Abhinavagupta says,
culminates in the identity-negation — and there the visibility is un-deviating. The jar's negation
rests on its identity being negated in that place, and the seeing that grounds it is whole. The
omniscient's seeing is not the limited seeing of the ordinary; it is the whole, un-broken perception of
the one who knows all.

So the vimarśa closes on the omniscient as the support of the powers. He sees all the atoms, all the
beings, all the interval — and his perception, being whole, establishes what is and what is not. The
limited seer, the arvāgdarśana, sees only a part; the omniscient sees the whole. And this omniscient —
the one whose perception is un-broken, whose non-perception establishes, whose support is all the
powers — is the maheśvara, the one knower in whom all the powers rest. With his establishment, the
seventh vimarśa — the reflexion on the one support of the powers — comes to its close.

**The great-Lordship: the freedom in the appearance-group**

The knower, with his powers of knowledge, memory, and removal, the inner-made-infinite-world-form, has
been established. Now Abhinavagupta asks what makes him *maheśvara*, the great Lord. The great-Lordship
(māheśvarya) is twofold: it is directed at objects of knowledge and at objects of action. Here, in the
jñānādhikāra, the knowledge-directed lordship is determined. What is the jñāna? It is the
self-experience "aham" — the "I" — contracted by the tint of the self-splitting appearance. And the
lordship is the *freedom in the appearance-group*: the freedom with which the appearances arise, vary,
and depend on one another.

The doubt arises at once. "All the dealing," the objector says, "is in the param-eśvara alone. But the
dealing's animator is one — there is nothing of its own beyond it. So what cause is there for the
varied dealing of the world, with all its clearness and variety?" And kārikā 1 answers: the appearances
are not all alike. Some are dependent on the eye's co-presence at that time — the "this jar," raised by
the impression's strength, depending on the perception that is near, sensory — and these appear in the
construction-dealing that follows immediately upon the perception. Others appear otherwise — in the
blind, in the darkness, and the rest, where there is no such eye-co-presence. The appearances are not
a single flat mass; they have their own dependence, their own conditions, their own arising.

And this is precisely the freedom. The varied dealing of the world is not caused by something outside
the Lord; it is the Lord's own freedom in the appearance-group — the freedom by which some appearances
depend on the senses, some do not, yet all are one. The appearance-group is not inert; it is the
manifestation of the Lord's freedom, the jñāna as the "aham" that shines through all the appearances,
unified in the one knower.

So the aṣṭamo vimarśa opens the great-Lordship. The Lord is maheśvara because he is free in the
appearance-group: the appearances arise, depend, and vary by his freedom, and yet they are one, because
they are all his own "aham"-manifestation. The knowledge-directed lordship is this freedom — the
self-experience that runs through all the appearances, the one "I" in which the whole world of
appearances rests. And this, Abhinavagupta will go on to show, grounds both the knowledge and the
action — the full great-Lordship of the one who is free in all the appearances, the maheśvara.

The jñānādhikāra — the whole first adhikāra of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī — comes to its
close. And it closes, fittingly, on the unity. It was said at the start that the one is the maheśvara;
now the unity is established. Kārikā 10: without that unity, the world-path of the consciousnesses
would not be; from the manifestation-unity, that one-ness, that one alone is the knower, it is
established.

The argument is simple and decisive. The whole dealing of the world — the path by which consciousnesses
know, remember, and act together — would be impossible if the consciousnesses were a scattered crowd of
mutually opaque streams. But the dealing is; so the consciousnesses must be one. And this is not hard to
accept, for the manifestation (prakāśa) is the very essence of the consciousnesses, and the
manifestation is one — there is no difference in the light itself. That one manifestation is, in truth,
the knower. The one light that shines in all the consciousnesses is the one knower, the param-essence
knower, the paramātman. Even the Sāṃkhya's and the Jaiminīya's self-luminous consciousness, and the
ancient Vaiśeṣika's consciousness-nature self, all point to this one.

The objection comes: "each cognition rests, in its own self-experience, in its own joining — what is
new here?" And the answer is that the known itself — the blue and the rest — has the manifestation as
its param-essence; the blue is, in its being, the light. So the unity is real, not a construction. And
the apparent difference of the known is made only by the māyā-power: the known-marker part, made
distinct from the manifestation as if it were other, is still the manifestation's own part. The
difference is the māyā's making; the unity is the truth.

And the Sāṃkhya's puruṣa — the separate self it posits — is not another at all. It is the un-recognized
own-lordship, the contracted consciousness; its knowledge and action, dealt as "I," are the
"I"-recollection. And this "I"-recollection, Abhinavagupta notes, is the pervader of all the states —
the pure, the mixed, the un-pure — gathered, not abandoned. The threefold self-recognition runs through
them all.

Then kārikā 11 sums up the whole: he alone, by the fixed reflexive-awareness-ness, is the great Lord;
the reflexive-awareness alone, of the God, in the pure knowledge-action, since. The great-Lordship is
nothing but the reflexive-awareness — the one who is aware of himself, fixedly, is the Lord; and that
reflexive-awareness is the God's own pure knowledge-and-action. The great-Lordship is not an added
power; it is the self-awareness itself, the "I" that knows and acts, the one knower.

And so the jñānādhikāra — the adhikāra on knowledge — is complete. The ||8|| colophon closes the
vimarśa on the great-Lordship in the one-support of the powers; and the great colophon reads:
"completed — this, the first jñānādhikāra." The first of the four adhikāras of the IPVV is done. It
has established the self, the powers, the one knower, the great-Lordship — all culminating in the
unity: the one manifestation is the one knower, and the one knower, aware of himself, is the Lord.

**Action, time and sequence: the timeless that manifests order**

Having established the nature of the power of knowledge, Abhinavagupta now turns to the power of
*action*. The two must run in parallel: if consciousness's power to know the world has been shown,
then its power to *effect* the world must be shown too. And here he must confront a paradox that sits
at the very heart of his system. The Lord is beyond time and sequence — utterly free of order — and
yet the world he manifests is shot through with sequence: causes before effects, moments before
moments, place before place. How can the timeless act in time?

He announces the answer in the opening verse of homage. He bows to Śiva, he says, "who, though free
of sequence, manifests manifold sequences." The whole doctrine is in that one image. And the image he
will use to make it work is the mirror. A mirror bears countless reflections — of things before it,
beside it, in all their variety — without ever ceasing to be the one, undivided mirror. It is not
torn into pieces by what it shows. So too the one consciousness, whose essence is nothing but
appearance, can take up within itself a host of seemingly contradictory forms — the ordered, distinct
appearances of the world — without its own oneness being divided in the least. This is the
"action-support" (kriyāśraya): the one that acts is one, and it is precisely *because* it is one and
un-divided that it can show sequence at all.

This is aimed squarely at the Buddhist. The Buddhist had said: only momentary cognitions flash
forth, in a stream, with no owner behind them; memory is nothing but impression; and cognition is
either inert — in which case it cannot reveal an object — or conscious, in which case it has no real
temporal distinctions, so there is no self that is anything other than this flux. Abhinavagupta
answers each point. Distinct cognitions cannot serve the ordinary dealings of the world — a string of
unrelated flashes could never get anyone to the village. Memory is not mere impression. And cognition
is the *un-contracted* consciousness, contracting itself by its own power under the tint of the
known object — and that self-contraction is what we call a "power" and a "dharma." It is one, it is
conscious, and it is not inert; and its oneness is no more threatened by its many appearances than a
mirror's is by its reflections.

So the first objection — "the action of the one is not ordered" — is rejected, precisely by
establishing that *one* as the agent. The one can be of many natures; that is not a contradiction.

But now a sharper objection. "Order is essential to action," the Buddhist says, "and how could order
be in the Lord, who is not cut through by time?" Here Abhinavagupta draws the crucial distinction. It
is the *worldly* action that is ordered. Consider the raising and lowering of a hand. Its earlier and
later moments are ordered; the single action that is the cause of the hand's moving from one position
to another — even if in itself eternal — is *inferred* as ordered, by the force of its ordered effect.
So the action of ordinary worldly dealing rightly rests in distinctions and is rightly called
ordered. What makes it so is the **time-power** (kālaśakti). And this time-power is nothing alien:
it is simply the Lord's own freedom, the freedom that raises the distinctions of appearance and lets
one thing follow another.

But the *Lord's own* action is a different matter. Because the Lord is not cut through by time, his
action is not cut through by time either: it is eternal, like the Lord himself. In the manifesting of
the known and the knower that underlies all our knowledge and dealing, the knowledge-power is the
capacity to reveal; but the reflexive-awareness-power — whose very self is freedom in joining and
separating — is, in truth, the action. And this action, though in reality free of all sequence,
*appears* ordered: it takes up the delimited forms of things in order to reveal the known, as if
casting the shadow of the known before it. It is the timeless showing time, the mirror showing order
while remaining one.

And so the paradox dissolves. The worldly action is ordered, by the time-power — which is the Lord's
freedom. The Lord's own action is eternal, un-cut by time. And the two are not in conflict, because
the sequence we see is precisely the Lord's timeless freedom manifesting itself as order — the mirror
showing many, while remaining one. This is the foundation on which the rest of the vimarśa — the
nature of time, the order of place, and finally the creation-power — will build.

  inert-or-conscious dilemma); Abhinava's three replies; the mirror image; kārikā 1's conclusion
  (establish the one agent, answer the objections); the nanu on order-in-the-Lord; the hand
  raising/lowering example; the worldly-action-is-ordered point; the time-power = Lord's freedom; the
  Lord's-own-action-is-eternal point; the "appears ordered to reveal the known."

  cannot-serve-dealing); "this time-power is nothing alien… it is the Lord's own freedom" (spells out

- **NOT resolved:** the truncated a. pra. si. 22 and "idam ityasya vicchinnavimarśasya" quotations

**Verdict:** understood and readable. The kriyādhikāra opens with a clear, coherent argument: the
timeless Lord manifests sequence without division (mirror), the worldly action is ordered by the
time-power (= the Lord's freedom), and the Lord's own action is eternal. The mirror is the load-bearing
figure that carries the whole opening.

What, then, is time? People point to the sun's course, the flowering of the seasons, heat and cold.
But in truth — Abhinavagupta insists — time is *order itself*. The Vaiśeṣika posits a time-substance,
the Sāṃkhya identifies it with rajas, the grammarians with an eternal, the Buddhist with the stream of
momentary being; but all of them, in the end, are describing the same thing: a *sequence*, a this-after-
that, projected outward and called "time." 

Consider how we actually measure. We measure gold by a fixed weight; we measure the day by the sun's
apparent course — "Caitra walks for a day." And the sun's own motion, in turn, is measured by the
water-clock. In every case, the "time" is nothing but the *fixed difference of nature* of some
appearance — the sun, the heat, the cuckoo — appearing as a measured sequence. And the power that makes
that sequence *appear*, that arranges appearances one after another, is the Lord's own power. Time is
therefore not a substance that cuts through things; it is order entering into appearance — the very
freedom of consciousness showing its appearances as before-and-after, as a dream or a magician's show
is arranged by the one who dreams it.

But is time merely *difference*? No — for then even the fingers, which differ, would have temporal
difference. What grounds order is deeper: it is the *being and not-being of appearances* — what is
manifest and what is not. Order is the difference between the spring that appears and the summer whose
appearance is withheld. And who withholds and reveals? The Lord, by his own *freedom* (svātantrya). He
manifests his appearances in every relation — the jar on the firm iron, the jar and the cloth as
distinct, or the two as one undivided juice — and it is only when he reveals the spring as empty of the
summer that order "blinks" into being. This power to manifest and to withhold is the **time-power**
(kālaśakti). So order, and time with it, is not a thing that imposes itself on the Lord; it is the
Lord's freedom, showing appearances as one-then-another. He is the stage-director of the world-machine,
who binds and releases, and so divides the universe into before and after.

The same freedom accounts for *place* as well as time. The variety of formed things — house, courtyard,
shop, shrine, garden, forest — gives rise to place-order, the extension and separation of things in
space. But place-order belongs to *many* things. Consider, by contrast, the ripening fruit: it is one
thing, yet it ripens — it passes through states one after another. That is time-order, and it belongs
to the *one*. The Lord, by his freedom, manifests the variety of actions — "Caitra goes," "the fruit
ripens" — and so brings time-order into being. And note where time lives: in the *known*, not in
consciousness. Even in a cognition, time touches only the known-part, the object as it appears — never
the self-awareness, the pure act of knowing, which is free of it.

Here is the crucial turn. Order — the being and not-being of appearances — belongs to the *finite*
knower, the one whose marker is the void-thought, the breath, the body. For his appearance is
*discontinuous* (vicchinna): his shining is not his own form; he is, as it were, inert, and it is only
consciousness flashing *as* him that lets him appear at all. Such a knower is always passing in and
out of manifestation, and so he is always in time. But the supreme knower — the one "once-shown"
(sakṛt), whose manifestation is continuous and un-broken — never has his appearances appear and
disappear. For him there is no before and after. Time does not touch him; and, since it is only with
reference to him that beings are in time, in the end time does not touch the beings either.

And the same must be said of place. The beings of the finite, *measured* knower shine as occupying
mutually exclusive places — this jar here, that body there. That is the finite knower's experience of
place. But the *immeasurable* knower — whose very self is manifestation, full by itself — has no such
division. His beings shine *in him*, like himself, un-measured, free of place-order. So with respect to
the pure self, the Lord has no place-order; and, by reference to him, neither do the beings. Time and
place, the two great frameworks of the world, are both, in the end, nothing but the Lord's freedom —
and they bind only the measured, the finite, the discontinuous; never the immeasurable, the
once-shown, the eternal.

The world, Abhinavagupta sums up, is the consciousness-dense self-filled — and this, the whole account
of time and order, is the statement of that self-fullness. And with this he turns to what comes next:
the *creation-power* (nirmāṇaśakti) of the thus-knowing Lord — the power by which the one who knows all
this actually creates the world. The foundation is laid: the Lord is one, free, timeless and placeless;
and time and place are but his freedom showing the world as order, binding only the measured and the
finite.

finite, discontinuous knower. The mirror/freedom images carry the whole vimarśa.

[chunk-v3-b-kriya-dvitiyo-k1-7-v35] The second vimarśa opens with a maṅgala and a seven-verse plan. The Lord's freedom, un-thwarted (apratihata), is to be established in the form of action-power (kriyāśakti): the action-relation and the related categories, which the external view cannot make fit, fit fully in this view. The first kārikā declares that the action, relation, universal, substance, direction, and time-cognitions are true — by stability and by use, as one-many-support.

The commentary explains why. The action-cognition that arises elsewhere than from consciousness-essence is mere action-appearance, cut off by māyā-power; but the action-essence as object is true, because the reflexive awareness resting on it is stable, not uprooted by the refuter, and agrees with the intended action. The being, in performing object-action, accepts distinction-non-distinction. Its un-deviable own-form is the form (mūrti); what, by appearance-strength, makes the non-own-form into own-form, is the action (kriyā). So Caitra's body, though divided by place, time, and form, manifests as "that very, this," and "Caitra goes" is the action. The reflexive awareness continuing in this is never uprooted, and the village-attainment is unbroken object-action. In the double-moon consciousness, by contrast, the reflexive awareness is uprooted, and the object is untrue by deficiency of object-action use, even if it causes delight or excitement.

The satya, asatya, and saṃvṛtisatya distinction is then drawn: the conventional-true is nothing of the general from its truth-ness, while the untrue is the double-moon and the like. The external action too is explained by action-power alone, so the external view's action is already accounted for. Stability is the always-helper; object-action use is the object-ness. The sūtra-meaning is brought in by joining the prior section with the other section, with the action taken as example.

The commentary then examines whether object-action-doing-ness is the being-ness's own-form, marker, or near-marker. Own-form-ness is metaphorical: branch-possessing alone is tree-ness, a mere exclusion, and the unreal does not do object-action. Marker-ness is shown not to hold: the marker is the un-deviability, mutually; otherwise over-extension and under-extension would result. Although direct-manifestation-cognition and construction-less consciousness are not synonyms, being distinct exclusions, they are marker and marked by mutual non-deviation. The others — the knowns — are then taken up, and the slice breaks off mid-sentence.

**The valid means: what establishes, and what it produces**

Abhinavagupta now turns to the heart of the relation between the known and the knower: the valid
means of cognition (pramāṇa). Everything in the world is established through a pramāṇa — nothing is
known without one — so before anything else we must determine what a pramāṇa is and what it yields.

In the world's ordinary usage, the answer seems simple. The object — the external blue, or the inner
pleasure — *by whose force* the cognition stands firm within its own fixed limit, as "this" (by its
own form) and "of-this-form" (by some further qualifying feature) — that object is called the valid
means. The blue itself, one might say, is what makes the cognition of blue valid.

But a moment's reflection undoes this. The object does not stand by its own power alone. If it did,
the blue would appear *to me* and not *to Caitra* — it would shine the same for everyone. It appears
to me, and so it stands by the power of *another*. And that other cannot be inert: an inert thing
could no more establish an appearance than a blind man could guide a blind man. So the other must be
of the nature of consciousness.

Yet mere consciousness is not enough either. An undifferentiated consciousness could never set blue
apart from yellow. What establishes the blue is a consciousness *tinted by* the blue, turned toward
the blue, shining *as* the blue — that appearance (ābhāsa) is what sets the blue before us. And the
blue it establishes is a *distinct* blue: if the blue were not distinct from consciousness, then the
very same consciousness, being one with everything, would have to be yellow too. So the appearance is
the shining of a distinct blue — even though, in the deepest sense, the blue is not other than the
great light of consciousness, the distinction appears nonetheless.

Now comes the grand unification. This whole arising — the contraction of the light by the limiting
conditions (the void, the body, the rest) — is *one single act* of the creation-power. And that one
act is precisely the illumination of the knower, the means, and the known together (pramātṛ, pramāṇa,
prameya). As the siddhapāda puts it: "the one light rises, born of means, object and knower." There is
not one power for knowing, another for the means, another for the object; it is all one light, one
manifestation.

So what, concretely, is the pramāṇa for us, the bound knowers? In the māyā-bound knower — contracted
by the body and the rest, turned inward — the appearance, as it were made distinct, faces the external
object. As long as it operates, it is tinted by the place and time of the object, changing from moment
to moment, a fresh rise each instant. And yet it is one and the same appearance, related to the one
knower, spanning endless time. That appearance — my appearance of blue — is the valid means, because it
is what does the work of producing the cognition of blue.

And what is that cognition — the fruit (pramiti)? It is, Abhinavagupta says, *the very same appearance*
turned inward: the awareness (bodhātmā) is the cognition, the fruit of the means. The means and the
fruit are not two separate things, nor are they mere synonyms. The means is the appearance facing
outward, of the nature of light; the fruit is the same appearance facing inward, of the nature of
reflexive-awareness, contracted by the tint of the object, taking the form of the word. In a single
thing the cause and its fruit are both discerned — as in the blue-light and its reflexive-awareness.
And the proof that the fruit is the reflexive-awareness is that the operation is the fruit (for the
instrument's first achievement is its operation), and the operation is non-different from the agent
being operated. So, in the primary sense, the means and the fruit are one; whatever *further* fruit
there is — the purpose served, the activity, the attainment — may be something else again. Hence the
reflexive-awareness is the fruit, and, by its force, the awareness is the means.

The reflexive-awareness, for its part, needs the word and rests in the general-form-appearance, free
of the mark of any particular place or time — that is its life. Even the bare "this" says only "what
is present, and before." So far as "Caitra stands here now" falls within the reach of words, that is
the path. It is by the force of the thing's own-marker-ness — like a direct perception of the speaker
— that one comes to rest in the specific. And this is the decisive point: **the pramāṇa's operation
is upon the appearance, and the appearance alone.** It does not seize the bare thing apart from all
manifestation; it works in and through the appearance.

- **Added (SUPPLIED, recoverable):** "nothing is known without one" (glosses pramāṇādhīnā vastusiddhi);

**Verdict:** understood and readable. The pramāṇavimarśa opens with a clean, coherent argument: the
pramāṇa is the appearance of a distinct object in consciousness (standing firm by its own conscious
power); its fruit is the reflexive-awareness of that same appearance turned inward; means and fruit are
one in the primary sense; and the means operates on appearance alone. This sets up the ten kārikās on
per-appearance operation that follow.

**How many appearances make one thing**

Abhinavagupta had concluded that the valid means operates *on the appearance alone*. But this raises
a pressing problem. The world treats things as *one* — the jar, the fire, the gold. If the means seizes
only an appearance, how can it ever reach the single thing those appearances belong to? And how can
many, ever-shifting appearances all belong to one and the same thing? The answer, developed across six
kārikās, turns on the *synthesizing awareness* — the one reflective grasp that gathers the many
appearances into one.

Take the jar. At first glance it is simply one. But reflect: the discriminating mind divides it. It
divides it according to our freedom, according to our wish, according to the conventions we have
learned. Looked at from one side it is long, from another round, from another upright; it is a being,
a substance, a jar, gold, a shining thing. So the one jar shows many appearances. What, then, keeps it
one? It is the *synthesis* (anusandhāna): the reflexive-awareness that is the very light by which all
these appearances shine. Sometimes this awareness rests in the single appearance and yields the
universal — the "jar-ness" that is the same in every jar; sometimes it mixes "this, of-this-form" and
is the synthesis that joins the appearances into the one thing. It is by the synthesis that the many
appearances of the jar are established as one jar.

The appearances, though divided by viewpoint, wish, and trained perception — the smoke and sandalwood
are known by a perception born of practice — are nevertheless *un-divided by place and time*. They all
belong here and now. So the divisions are not of the thing's being somewhere at some time; they are
divisions of how it appears, gathered by the one awareness.

Now the subtlety of the object-action. When appearances mix, one of them is primary and is the common
locus (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the others. Quickened by the sentence-awareness "this here, now, is the
jar," the appearances that have attained one own-marker-ness — without abandoning their difference —
do their object-actions. Some actions belong to the aggregate; some are fixed, each to each, singly.
The important point: it is the *object-action* that makes a thing real in the world's sense. And many
appearances can do *one* object-action. Here is the image Abhinavagupta gives. Separate lamp-lights do
not, of themselves, light up a single dwelling; but gathered in one house, they do one thing — they
make it bright. Streams, falling separately into the ocean with their countless waves, nevertheless as
a whole do one thing. So the jar, the gold, the red, the great — their several appearances together
produce a single object-action, say the great delight fit for bathing the image of Śiva. And the doer
of that one effect must be one. The one cognition, the one reflexive-awareness, is marked by the one
object-action.

And what about the fire — its heat, its denotation as "fire"? Here Abhinavagupta draws the crucial
distinction between what needs nothing else and what depends on another. The heat-appearance of the
fire is *un-opposed, un-created, fixed everywhere and always* — it needs no other object. But the
fire-as-fuel, the fire-as-cause-of-smoke — these *depend on another object* (the fuel, the smoke).
And the very meaning of the word "fire" is fixed by convention. All of these — the heat, the denotation
— are the fire's own-form (svabhāva), and they are established by the *one* valid means: the single
perception that looks, as it were, to the glance of the determinative power (niyati). So even though
the means seizes the appearance, the thing's own-form — what makes the fire fire and not something
else — is fixed, and known through the one perception.

The conclusion of the whole sequence: the pramāṇa operates on appearance, but it does not lose the
thing. The one synthesizing awareness gathers the many appearances into the one thing; the one
object-action confirms its reality; and the niyati-power fixes its own-form. The one and the many are
not in conflict — they are two phases of the same appearance, gathered by the awareness and fixed by
the power. This is the distinction-and-non-distinction doctrine, applied to the valid means itself.

- **Preserved:** the per-appearance operation of the pramāṇa; the one jar divided by freedom/wish/

**The primacy of the knower: error, difference, and the ground of all cognition**

We have established that the valid means operates on the appearance. But this opens the deepest
problem of all. If the means seizes only appearances, how do we ever tell the *true* from the *false*
— the real jar from the illusory double-moon, or the shell from the silver it is mistaken for? And if
the synthesizing awareness gathers many appearances into one thing, why is not every appearance real?
The answer Abhinavagupta builds across these nine kārikās is the crowning claim of the whole vimarśa:
error is a matter of the reflexive-awareness, difference and non-difference are real, and in the end
it is the *knower* who is the ground of everything — so that in the supreme knower, no valid means is
needed at all.

First, the one and the many means. The objection arises: if the means operates on the appearance, and
if the appearance is gathered into one, is there after all only one means? No, Abhinava answers. The
perception that grasps a quality is not the same thing as the inference from a sign; they differ in
object and in form. It is the *collective* of the means that does the work — not a single one.

Now the far and the near. The thing I saw far off as a whole, I now see near at hand with all its
details. How is it one? Because of the one recognition — the reflexive-awareness "this is the very
thing I saw before." That primary manifestation, by which the earlier and later appearances are joined,
is what keeps the thing one, however variously it appears. The "shadow" of difference lies in the
appearing, never in the essence of the manifestation itself, which is reflexive-awareness through and
through. And this is the key to truth and falsity: the distinction is not made by the pramāṇa's being
un-contradicted, but by the *reflexive-awareness'* being un-contradicted.

What about the object-action — the capacity of a thing to do what we expect of it? It is not the
thing's own form; nor is it independent — it depends on the Lord's will and fixity. So the thing does
not collapse into unreality, nor become another thing, merely because a given object-action does not
come about. The jar is still the jar, the designating word still designates it, even if the external
object-action is absent.

But now the shell-silver — the classic case of error. If the one-recognition makes things one, why is
the shell-not-silver not also real? Because, although the shell and the silver are recognized as one,
the silver that flashes in the mind has *no standing* as the real silver. It is not the external,
real, universally-dealing, saleable silver. And the reflexive-awareness that posits it is *uprooted*:
by the non-agreement of this place — this is a shell, not silver — the awareness "this form is not
silver" is stable and uproots the false one. Disagreement (asaṃvāda) is precisely this: a cognition
opposed to the correct manifestation-reflexive-awareness. So too with the double-moon: the region of
the sky where a second moon appears is re-cognized as "here there is no second moon," and the false
awareness is uprooted. Error, then, is not a failure to be a real appearance; it is an appearance whose
reflexive-awareness is uprooted. Truth and falsity are decided by the standing or falling of the
reflexive-awareness.

Next, difference and non-difference. The beings shine with both a continued and an excluded self —
the cow is like other cows (class, non-difference) and unlike them (qualities, word — difference).
Neither the continuation nor the exclusion can be faulted, for there is no supreme reality that would
refute either; both shine by the freedom of experience. The difference is by the qualities and the
word; the non-difference by the class. And both, Abhinavagupta insists, rest in the *one knower* — the
one who re-cognizes, who holds the before and after together. The difference, no less than the
non-difference, is real only in the Lord, who is capable of re-cognizing the very limit of that
difference. The whole pramāṇa-marker, in fact, points to the **primacy of the knower** (pramātṛ-
pradhāna): the knower is the ground, and the means is his operation.

And this leads to the great conclusion. The appearance was said to be the pramāṇa for the *contracted*
knower. But in the param-essence-real Lord — whose form is mere manifestation, always shining — how
could there be a pramāṇa? The world-variety rests in him as a picture rests on an even wall: the wall
shows the painted elevations and hollows without itself being raised or hollow. So the whole
distinction-and-non-distinction of the world rests in the always-shining Lord, untouched by his being
or not-being. And in that *ancient* knower (purāṇa), whose form is always manifested, there is no
valid means and no new appearance — for the manifestation is his very essence, and it cannot fail to
be. All the cognitions (pramitis) rest in him; there is no separate perception or inference that could
establish what is always self-shining. The means is, in every case, the new appearance — and it serves
only the finite, contracted knower. In the supreme knower, means and result are transcended: he is the
ground from which all dealing, all knowing, all acting is operated, by the mere manifestation of his
power.

**Grace, initiation, and the one liberated while living**

All that has been established — the valid means, its fruit, the primacy of the knower — now comes to
its practical point. How does one actually attain the Lord? The whole vimarśa closes with the answer:
by the Lord's grace, working through a fourfold effort, and culminating in the one liberated while
still living.

There is a supreme work to be accomplished. Even if it seems impossible in itself, it is undertaken
as possible; and the effort that drives it is the life of the fourfold work. But the decisive factor is
not the effort alone — it is the *grace* of the Lord. Only when the Lord's self is pleased, when the
turbidity of our conceit in the body and the rest is abandoned, are we able to cross the great ocean
of delusion. The means are laid out in the Lord-taught teaching: the initiatory rite (dīkṣā), the
vision-yoga (dhyāna), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhāvanā). By their combined capacity, the
aspirant abandons the world that is to be left behind — the knower-made world of body, breath, the
eight-fold city and the void, the world of the things that support and objectify enjoyment — and,
through the grace of the Lord and the guru, brings the lordship itself to manifestation within his own
self.

The order matters. Although vision and knowledge are primary, knowledge is preceded by initiation. As
the teaching says, there is no eligibility for the yoga of Śaṅkara without the dīkṣā; and the dīkṣā is
twofold, by rite and by knowledge. But what if one, assured by the knowledge-initiation alone, has not
practiced the vision-yoga? Then there is devotion (bhāvanā). Some, the yogins, attain a share of the
wondrous powers — a portion of all-knowing and all-doing, the eight-fold vibhūti, pertaining to this
or that world. But even where such powers are manifest, nothing of the present goal is lost; and this,
too, is established by reason.

Now a subtle point about the self. The prāṇa — the vital breath, the body, the rest — is experienced
as "I." How is this compatible with the param-ātman, the supreme self? There is no conflict, because
the two are present together. The prāṇa's being felt as "I" is nothing other than the supreme self's
own free manifestation: the param-ātman shines freely, and by that very shining the prāṇa and the
rest appear as "I." Even the knower-ness that touches them is that same light. The object is
remembered, because experience is broken and re-collected; but the knower — whose essence is the
un-broken light — is not something that could be remembered. As the Spandakārikā says, remembered-ness
is not how the essence is realized. So the Lord-ness is not a new thing to be proved in the
consciousness-essence; and the negation of "I" in the breath and the body is not a new discovery
either. Both were there from the beginning.

And so the end. In all this there is the utter extinction of the delusion-impression. And when that
is extinguished, when the restraint of the body-and-"I" conceit dissolves, there is the Lord-ness
itself. Yet even here, by the Lord's will alone, for some the recognition does not arise despite a
hundred efforts. But even for such a one, merely by coming to hear the teaching, by the ordered
ripening of the impression, there is necessarily the attainment of one's own form. The āgama declares:
"Unwavering in self-experience, he is called the jīvanmukta, the one liberated while living; but he
who still constructs the essence — at the fall of the body, he goes to Śiva." And Abhinavagupta adds
his own verse: the sparks of the pure-knowledge-fire blaze when the inner intent is ended, like the
root-leaves of the old tree of saṃsāra caught in the fire of the supreme reality.

Hence, by all this, **nothing new is established in the self**. The Lord was always the own self;
grace, initiation, vision, knowledge and devotion only reveal what was already there. This, Abhinavagupta
says, is what was declared at the very beginning of the teaching — in the agent, the knower, the own
self, the ādi-siddha, the already-established. The tṛtīyo vimarśa — the reflexive-awareness of the
valid means, its fruit, and the supreme truth of the known — here comes to its close.

**Causality is the conscious knower's agency**

In the previous vimarśa the relation between the known and the knower was shown to be the very
expansion of the action-power. Now Abhinavagupta turns to the other great relation: cause and effect.
And he announces his thesis without hesitation: **the essence of cause and effect is nothing but the
relation of agent and object of action.** Causality, in the end, is the agency of a conscious knower.
Everything that follows — eleven kārikās of argument against the inert, the Buddhist, and the Sāṃkhya
— serves to prove that single claim.

It begins with the Lord. This ancient knower manifests the world of beings without break. How does he
do it? By his will — the un-divided, un-ordered will that is non-different from him. And where are
these beings for him? In his infinite power: all beings are, ultimately, his own powers. This
will-driven manifesting is precisely his action, his making, his creating. The objection — "if the
will is eternal, then creation and destruction would be simultaneous; if occasional, then it needs
another cause" — is answered: the will is tinted by the particular thing to be made, and so it is not
simultaneous with everything at once.

Now the hard work: to show that the *inert* cannot be a cause. Take the seed and the sprout. The
inert seed cannot endow the sprout with being — for the sprout is either already existent (in which
case nothing is acquired) or non-existent (in which case it cannot come to be, since the non-existent
has no nature by which to gain existence). The claim that the effect is both existent and non-existent,
or neither, is self-contradictory. The blue cannot become yellow, however hard we try; so the
non-existent cannot acquire existence. Hence the inert, material cause has no real causal power. The
real cause is elsewhere.

The cause, Abhinavagupta argues across the next kārikās, is the *conscious*. The potter creates the
pot by his power; the yogin, by his will alone, brings about an effect without any clay or seed. If
the inert seed and clay were the true causes, this would be impossible. But it is not impossible —
which shows that the true cause is consciousness, the free will that shapes the effect. The whole
apparatus of the inner and outer, the two appearances, resolves into this: the effect arises from the
conscious knower's will, and ultimately from the Lord.

And what of inference — the way we come to know causes at all? Here Abhinavagupta examines the
own-nature reason (svabhāvahetu). It has two kinds. In the first, the cause-effect relation is clear
and embryonic: "it is fiery because it is smoky," where fire is the cause of smoke. In the second, the
relation is reversed. Take the famous example: the śiṃśapā, a kind of tree. From "this is a śiṃśapā"
we infer "this is a tree." But here there is no *otherness* — the śiṃśapā-ness is not a separate thing
from the tree-ness; it *is* the tree-ness in a specific form. So the entailment holds (wherever the
śiṃśapā-ness is, the tree-ness is), even though the genuine causal relation that requires two distinct
things is absent. This is the basis of all inference: the cause is necessarily present with the
effect, fixed by the determinative power. And the śiṃśapā, born from its own seed by the rule that a
thing arises from its own full complement of causes, is precisely the śiṃśapā-ness that excludes
non-tree-ness.

The upshot: causality, even at the level of inference, is grounded in a real, necessary relation —
not in the power of the inert. The Buddhist's and the Sāṃkhya's accounts of causality, far from
threatening this, actually rest on the same basis when understood rightly. And this entire edifice
shows that the agency of the knower — which is the essence of causality — is not something that could
belong to a limited, non-lordship being. It requires the Lord. Causality, in the end, is the Lord's
will at work: the relation of agent and object of action, expanded through the whole world.

**Inference across knowers, and the mirror of consciousness**

We have said that causality is the conscious knower's agency. But this draws a sharp objection from
the Buddhist idealist, the Vijñānavādin. "If everything is appearance," he says, "then cause and
effect are only relations *between appearances*. An un-manifested fire is nothing at all. So how can
the smoke-appearance arise from it? And how can you infer the fire from the smoke?"

Abhinavagupta's answer is subtle and rests on the one creation. The Vijñānavādin, holding each
conscious stream to have its own private appearances, could find cause and effect only within his own
smoke-and-fire appearances — he can never reach another's. But in our view this is wrong. The Lord
creates the appearances *for all the knowers at once, as one*. So when we grasp the pervasion — that
smoke implies fire — the smoke-appearance and the fire-appearance belong, in the Lord's single
creation, to every knower alike. The smoke-appearance arises from the fire-appearance, and this
pervasion can be grasped, once, for all. And for the whole range of knowers — from the worm to the
omniscient — the fire-appearance is one, not split by the difference of streams; so the smoke can
arise from it and from nothing else. That fire-appearance, being indirect to the one who infers, is
what we call the "cause of the Lord" (adhipatipratyaya); it is new, not like the smoke that is born of
smoke. It is the non-wandering, effect-marker, by which the inference is actually made. So inference
holds across knowers, because the Lord has created the appearances as one.

Now, the dependence of cause and effect — the "in-this-existing-this-is" that the pervasion expresses.
Here Abhinavagupta is careful. The dependence is not a real *otherness* between two separate things.
The fire and its heat: their distinction is only constructed. The fire, as the shining own-marker,
cannot have the heat as a separate own-form — both are of equal cause, both come from the one reality.
So in truth the dependence is one, quickened by the synthesis, by the awareness that joins them. The
grammatical point — the locative "in fire [there is] heat" — is not meaningless, nor does it point to
a merely fabricated referent; it is real, and it is supported by the one knower. The dependence of
cause and effect is not two things leaning on each other; it is one thing known as one.

But what if the Sāṃkhya, with its own account of transformation, offers a better story? Here
Abhinavagupta shows that even the Sāṃkhya's "dry" cause-and-effect is not dry. The Sāṃkhya says: there
is one substance — the seed, or the primal principle — with an ordered variety of natures; the earlier
nature is the cause, the later is the effect; the whole evolves by transformation (pariṇāma). But
Abhinavagupta's point is that the transformation itself is an *action*. The transition from the
earlier nature, given up, to the later nature, newly unfolded, is precisely the agent-act-object
structure — the freedom of transforming, which is agency. So even in the Sāṃkhya view, causality is
not the dry change of a thing; it already contains the free knower's act. The intellect, the earth, the
sprout — all are states of the one substance, and the transformation that runs through them is an
action.

And finally, the great closing argument — why only *consciousness* can bear difference and
non-difference at all. The inert, Abhinavagupta says, is a fixed form. It is a known object, and as a
known object it is "different" with respect to another thing (the blue as against the non-blue) and
"non-different" with respect to itself. But the *very same* nature cannot be both different and
non-different — that is a contradiction. So the inert, being a known object, cannot be many-natured.
But consciousness is different. It does not fall into the state of a known object. Like a clear, free
mirror, it bears the whole variety of appearances as its *reflections* (pratibimba) — and those
reflections are distinct, even within the one mirror, without the mirror being torn apart. So
difference-and-non-difference — the very structure of the world, the cause in the effect, the one in
the many — fits only in consciousness, never in the inert.

The objection — "then why don't the elephant and the mountain, appearing in the one, conflict with its
one-ness?" — is answered: because they are *in the mirror*. They do not touch the mirror's own form;
they are its reflections. And the free mirror shows all, even by its mere limpidity alone. This is its
might. The whole vimarśa thus closes on the mirror-image of consciousness: the one reality that can
bear the world's difference-and-non-difference, because it is a free, clear light that reflects all
without being divided by any reflection.

**The will as cause, agent, and action**

The whole vimarśa has argued that causality is the conscious knower's agency. Now comes the sharpest
objection of all, and it threatens to undo everything. If consciousness is *one* — if all the world is
a single consciousness and the difference of things is only ignorance — then how is action possible at
all? For action needs an agent and an object, two distinct things; but if all is one, there is no
distinct object for the agent to act upon.

Abhinavagupta's answer is that action is the one *will-to-do* that joins the agent and the object. The
jar and the consciousness are, by appearance, two. But there is a single re-recollection (parāmarśa)
marked by the will-to-do — the moment "I will make this" — which rests, as it were, in the other
consciousness-essence and binds the two together. It is this one will-recollection, and not any
external contact, that makes the jar an object of action and consciousness its agent. Without it there
is no action, even in a perfectly unified consciousness.

But here Abhinavagupta turns on the very idea that the difference is a mere "ignorance." If
consciousness is one, and the difference is ignorance, then we must ask: *of whom* is this ignorance?
The one-form Brahman cannot have an ignorance that is the mere absence of something else. Nor can the
separate souls exist — they too would be raised up by the ignorance. If the ignorance is called
"un-explainable" (anirvācya), then we still do not know whose it is; "it shines and yet is
un-explainable" is the speech of a yakṣa, a being we cannot pin down. And in fact the difference is
real: our cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference, and the very "refutation"
that would remove difference is itself a manifestation — and so would be difference, and so would be
ignorance. The whole attempt to dismiss the world as an un-explainable illusion cuts the horns of the
hare's head and plucks the sky-flower. Even if we appeal to the revealed teaching, that teaching too
would be ignorance — a net of illusions. (And indeed, as Abhinavagupta will say, "even Brahman with
ignorance is [admitted by some], so this is not an absolute monism either.")

What, then, of the division of the powers — will in the Lord, knowledge in Sadāśiva, action in Īśvara?
This is not a separation of real things; it is one action-power, seen under different aspects. The
action-power in the action is nothing other than the will. As the teaching says, "the three subtle
powers dwell in harmony." And the grammarians' own analysis confirms it: the action-tattva is seen in
the agent even when the other adjuncts are absent, and is not seen when the agent's complement is
absent — so by presence-and-absence, it is the *resting in the agent* alone that is the action. Even
where no explicit agent appears — "here it does not cook" — the agents fit for cooking and enjoying are
manifest, implied by the locus. Action is not a thing that happens to an inert object; it is the will
at rest in the knower.

And so the final synthesis: the will (icchā) itself is the cause-ness, the agent-ness, and the action.
The three are one act of consciousness. The cause does not cause, the agent does not act, the action
does not move — all three are the one will, by which the Lord, wishing to stand, becomes the world of
jar and cloth and all the appearances. This is the action-power: the will of the one consciousness,
which is at once what causes, what acts, and what is done. With this, the fourth vimarśa of the
kriyādhikāra — the reflexive-awareness of the cause-effect relation — comes to its close.

**The teaching as the measure: the categories from the Lord's word**

The action-power, we have seen, has as its very form the un-clouded manifestation of all the
categories of the world. But this raises the question the kriyādhikāra could not answer: *what* are
these categories, these tattvas? Our perception is not an omniscient eye; our inference lacks the
pervasion that would reach every thing. Neither can grasp the whole. Only the **āgama** — the revealed
teaching — can do so; for it is nothing other than the re-recollection of the un-contracted
manifestation of the supreme Lord, and so it alone can measure the entire universe. As the rule has it:
the one valid means is that utterance, true, spoken by the Lord; its word is not to be refuted by the
gross means of men. And this is why Abhinavagupta now opens a new section, the āgamādhikāra: to expound
the categories from the Lord's own teaching, aided by reasoning.

The theme is announced at once. All this creation is *warp and woof* (otaprota) — the categories from
Śiva down to the earth are woven into the one reality. And at the heart of it all is the **Śivatattva**,
which is the body of every category. The cause-and-effect relation does not rest in the inert; it rests
in the consciousness-form, whose essence is manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness. By its freedom this
consciousness shines both within and without, raising the order of time; and in the form of the
knowledge-power it becomes the substrate that takes on the ordered operation as its own action-power.
So knowledge and action — manifestation and reflexive-awareness — are un-joined, inseparable; and this
inseparable pair is the supreme form of all beings. This is the Śivatattva: the one that, through the
gate of the action-power, takes up the whole fivefold work, and, being taught for our devotion,
appears as the appearance-form of everything.

The objection comes: "How can Śiva, who is beyond māyā, appear as the *primary* category in the world
of mind?" The answer: self-shining is freedom, and the downward-pervasion of that self-shining is
creation itself. The self-shining Śiva, in his freedom, pours himself downward into the world — and
that pouring is the world. There is nothing arbitrary here; it is the very nature of the light to shine
forth.

From this one reality, the categories unfold in order. When the *inner* state — the knowledge-form —
surges, we have the **Sadākhya** (also called Sadāśiva), the first category, from which the cognition
"is, is" (sad, sad) shines: the pure self aware of the world as its own. When, on the other hand, the
*outer* being — the action-power form — becomes primary, we have the **Īśvara-tattva**, established
after the Sadākhya, in which the impossible-doing of the Lord appears as its great power. Both are the
one reality, seen under its inner and outer aspect, like a picture just unclosed (the pure group) or
like the full painted picture (the Īśvara).

Below these pure categories come the impure ones. There is the **śuddhavidyā** (the true knowledge),
where the "I" and the "this" are co-referent — the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of self and world.
And then, descending, the categories manifest as *non-self* (anātma) — as objects rather than as the
self. This is the "un-param-ness" (āparatva) of the beings: the lower categories appear as other than
the self. Even the distinction-cognition (bhedadhī), the cognition of difference, belongs to the
awareness of the agent and carries us further into the divided world. And the lordship-nature
(aiśvarya), when it is manifested in the *animal* being — the bound knower — shows the Lord's nature
in the state of bondage, setting up the great distinction of the bound and the Lord that will occupy
the rest of this vimarśa.

So the āgamādhikāra begins by tracing the categories downward from the one reality — the Śivatattva,
the body of all, through the pure group (Sadāśiva, Īśvara, śuddhavidyā) into the impure, the
non-self, the divided, and the bound. All of it, warp and woof, is the one consciousness shining forth;
and the teaching — the Lord's own re-recollection — is the measure that grasps it whole.

**The coverings and the categories of the known**

Descending from the pure realm, we come to the world of the bound knower. Here the pure self is not
seen as it is; it is covered by a set of limiting sheaths — the *kañcukas*, literally the "armours" or
"coverings." These are niyati (fixity), kāla (time), rāga (attachment), vidyā (the limited knowledge),
and kalā (the limited agency). In the bound state, the one-flavored reality is seen as divided, and
the self's "I-ness" is mistakenly found in what is not the self — in the body, the breath, the mind.

Take the first of these, niyati, the fixative power. In the world we say: the seed is the cause of the
sprout, not of the pot; the clay is the cause of the pot, not of the sprout. This apparent *fixing* of
each effect to its own cause — this is niyati. But Abhinavagupta's point is that this fixity, which
seems to be a feature of the things themselves, in truth belongs to the *knower*, not to the known. In
reality the Lord alone shines forth as "this is the cause of that"; the binding of each cause to its
effect, as it appears, is a covering laid over the reality by the limited knower. So too with time,
and with attachment — the whole flux of the mind, rooted in desire and envy, is the rāga-covering.
These are the armours that hide the pure self in the bound state.

The bound knower — the one whose being is measured by the void-thought, the breath, the body — is the
one who knows the separated objects. He is the māyīya knower, the knower in the realm of māyā, facing
outward toward the distinct things of the world. And the objects he knows are the categories of the
*known* (prameya), which are counted as twenty-three.

They fall into three groups. First, the one *pradhāna* — the root-cause, the un-divided matter out of
which the world evolves (in the Sāṃkhya manner). Second, the *thirteen organs* — the external and
internal instruments of knowing and acting: the five senses, the five organs of action, and the inner
organ with its aspects of mind, ego and intellect. Third, the *ten-fold effect-group* — the five
subtle elements (tanmātras) and the five gross elements, distinguished as subtle and gross. These
twenty-three, Abhinavagupta notes, are the known in the impure realm.

But he adds an important caveat. These categories — the pradhāna, the subtle and gross elements — are
not truly graspable by the common-marker, the ordinary perception of the world. They are not
sensible in the ordinary way; and even their "instrument-ness" is not fitting in the usual sense. So
the categories of the known, in the bound realm, are not things we perceive plainly; they are the
structure of the divided world, laid out by the māyā-power over the one reality.

And so the prathamo vimarśa of the āgamādhikāra comes to its close. It has traced the categories from
the Śivatattva — the body of all — down through the pure group and into the impure realm, where the
self is covered by the kañcukas and the world is divided into the twenty-three categories of the
known. All of it, in the end, is the one consciousness, woven warp and woof, hidden from the bound
knower by the coverings that are themselves, in truth, aspects of the knower rather than of the things.
This sets the stage for the next vimarśa, which will analyze the bound and the Lord (paśu and pati) in
their full distinction.

**The knowers and the stains that bind**

We have set out the categories of the known — the world that is known. But the heart of this whole
teaching is the recognition of the Lord in the self; and to recognize him we must understand the
*knowers* themselves. For there are many knowers, from the bound to the pure, and they are distinguished
by the stains that bind them. Abhinavagupta opens this vimarśa with a homage to the one "who wields the
trident, cutting the three nooses" — and those three nooses are the three stains (mala) that will
occupy him throughout: the stain of finitude (āṇava), the stain of objectivity (māyīya), and the stain
of action (kārma).

The knower-states have their presiding deities. In the pure state — where the knower stands in his mere
knower-ness, the objects withdrawn — the presider is **Rudra**: the supreme Śiva, who as the Lord
brings his worshippers into that state, and who, even within the realm of māyā, is the one with the
opened third eye. But in the spread of the *distinct* world, the presiders are **Brahmā** and **Viṣṇu**:
Brahmā in the production of the spread, Viṣṇu in its flowing continuation. And the difference is this:
these two make the "this" — the object — primary, and the "I" — the knower-essence — subordinate;
whereas the pure Rudra makes the "I" primary. They are not third-eyed, as the Rudra is. Yet even these
Brahmā and Viṣṇu forms are not something apart from the Lord: they shine as the qualities of the
intellect, not as the pure consciousness itself; their form is the lordship — the freedom, the
knowledge, the action-power — standing as the support of the world.

Now the bound knower. He is the one blind by māyā, wandering in saṃsāra, bound by his actions. This is
the paśu, the animal — the knower who has lost his freedom. And over against him stands the pati, the
Lord: the knower whose own-members — the beings of the world — are his own. The bound one is bound
because he has suffered the *loss of freedom* of the awareness: he has become un-aware of his own
freedom, and so he is caught in the objects. This is the working of the māyā: the manifestation of the
distinct known — the world spread out as other than the self — which gives us birth and enjoyment, and
which is the māyīya stain.

The knowers come in grades. There are the pure ones — those who, even in the unity of the
awareness-marker, are mutually distinct, and who lack the *highest* agency: these are the vidyeśvara
group. There are the pralayākala — the "dissolved" ones, absorbed in the state of dissolution, who have
only the stain of finitude, their form the un-awareness of the void and the rest. And even the aware
ones, who possess agency, still stand in the stain of action. Indeed, all the becoming ones — the gods
and men and the rest — have the three-fold stain: finitude, objectivity, action. And binding them all
is the kalā — the limited agency — which raises the consciousness-essence into the narrow form of the
individual agent.

So the picture is complete. Beneath the Lord, who is free and whole, lie the many knowers, bound each
by his stain: the finitude that shrinks the infinite self into a single soul, the māyā that spreads the
world out as other, and the action that keeps the soul bound in the round of birth and enjoyment. It is
these three nooses that the trident-bearing Lord cuts. And to understand how they are cut — how the
bound knower can be released into the recognition of his own lordship — Abhinavagupta will turn next to
the states and the entry, the samāveśa, through which the bound one rises to his true nature.

**The states of the bound knower, and the way to the fourth**

The knower, at bottom, is nothing other than the free conscious agent — his agency, his awareness, and
his consciousness-self are primary. But the bound knower does not live in that freedom. He lives in a
round of states — waking, dream, and deep sleep — which are the very texture of his bondage. To
understand these states, and which of them lead him to his true nature, is the concern of this closing
part of the vimarśa.

At the lowest extreme is the state of the void. In the emptiness — where the intellect and the rest are
absent — the "I-ness" and the "agent-ness" are only words. This is the dissolved knower, the
pralayākala, absorbed in the void, with only the barest trace of an "I." His is a sleep without even a
dream.

Above that, the vital breath (prāṇa) stirs: it is the inner operation that stimulates the senses, the
life that links the self to the organs. And with the breath come the three great states. Deep sleep
(suṣupta) is like dissolution — a resting in the mere void or in the breath, where consciousness is put
to sleep by māyā and not awakened even by the limited agency (kalā) or the limited knowledge (vidyā).
It has two grades: with the known (the vidyākalā, still touched by the māyā-stain) and without the
known (the pralayākala, free of the stain). Its many forms — sleep from fatigue, fainting from shock,
intoxication and madness from wine, and even samādhi, the sleep of the yogin won by effort — are all
species of this one deep-sleep state.

The dream (svapna) is different. In the dream the senses are fixed and still, yet one sees the beloved
and reaches out to touch her. Here only the mind is active, drawing on the prior creation, and making a
clear, vivid world of its own — a momentary creation of the Lord within the dreamer. But in its
sense-object part the dream shares the common world; and the moment we wake, the dream's clarity is
refuted. So the dream is the mind's own making, a clear-appearance that the waking refutes.

The waking state (jāgrat) is the common creation — the firm, external world shared by all the knowers.
The waking knower is one who has shaken off the delusion-causing sleep. And yet, even here, the dream-
form persists within the waking: the five states interpenetrate, each containing traces of the others.
It is the difference of the known, Abhinavagupta notes, that spins out these many states of the one
knower-ness.

Now the crucial point. These three states — waking, dream, deep sleep — are to be *abandoned* by the
seeker of liberation. For they are bound up with the vital breaths, with the primary-ness of the
prāṇa in the agent, and with the rise and fall of pleasure and pain. The seeker, seeing this, regards
the whole threefold round as the sphere to be left behind. The breath and the out-breath (prāṇa and
apāna) run through waking and sleep; the udāna goes upward through the middle; but beyond them all is
the fourth — the turya — the state that goes beyond the three, of the fire-form, the pure consciousness
that is the goal. It is into this fourth that the recognition leads the bound knower, out of the round
of the three, into the freedom that was always his own.

With this, the dvitīyo vimarśa of the āgamādhikāra — the analysis of the knowers, the stains, and the
states — comes to its close. The bound soul has been fully mapped: its stains, its grades, its states,
and its breaths. And the way out has been shown: through the recognition, from the three abandoned
states to the fourth, the fire-form, the free consciousness-self.
