**The collection of the essence: the one Lord, and how the many arise**

The whole teaching — the self-manifest consciousness, the knowledge-action power, the maheśvara —
has been set out at length through three adhikāras. Now Abhinavagupta gathers it into a brief
collection, the tattvārthasaṅgraha, in fifteen verses, so that the student can hold it in mind and
mediate upon it. One verse states the supreme essence; nine give the bond of the knower and the known;
five give the liberation, which is the recognition. And it all begins with the single great claim.

The own-self alone of all beings is the one Lord, the maheśvara. He is the world-form, and his
re-recollection — "I, this" — is un-broken. This is not a doctrine; it is the discovery of the very
flashing of the self. As the teaching says, all beings are Śiva — the self of all beings is Śiva — and
the self-flashing in each is the Lord. So the first word of the collection is: you are that one.

But then how does the many arise? In the own-self, in the one Lord, by his freedom, a "this-part" is
created, preceded by a contraction. In its midst, the intellect, the breath, the body — known as
"this" — and by the this-ness of that distinct-known, an "I-being" shines, the grasper. He who says
"I am happy," who grasps himself as this contracted being — that is the bound one. And his liberation
is precisely the recognition of what he truly is.

The bound one is "the many person." For truly, nothing is bound: in truth there is only the one free
Śiva, consciousness-natured. But when consciousness contracts and manifests itself as this finite
body and this passing breath, there arises the un-cognition of its own complete form — and with that,
the many persons, each caught in the round of action and enjoyment, which appears to him as pleasure
and as suffering. The one becomes the many; the free becomes the bound; and all through the simple
forgetting of what one is.

The Lord, however, remains whole. In the Lord, everywhere, the manifestation and the reflexive-awareness
are the knowledge and the action; and the māyā-power, which opens up the "this-ness" of things, is
only the covering that lets the world appear. But in the bound one, in the state of self-forgetting,
these very powers appear perverted: the pure manifestation becomes the "being-ness," the rajas of
activity, the darkness of inertia. So the qualities of the world — the sattva, rajas, tamas of the
Sāṃkhya — are nothing but the Lord's own powers, seen in the mirror of the bound soul.

Hence the power-ness is not declared from mere distinction. The bound person, taking himself as one
enjoyer among many, thinks the qualities to be distinct things; but in truth they are the power-form
of the Lord. The being, the bliss, and the action belong to the Lord; in the animal, what appears is
their absence — the two-own mixture of the rajas, the suffering, the attached, the covering.

And yet even here the Lord is present. Even in the mixed and the distinct appearances, in the very
"this-ness" of the world, there is the non-conventional, innate this-ness-recollection of the Lord.
The emptiness itself, the void that the seeker meets, is the Rudra-presided — manifesting as the
negation of the "I." For the animal, however, the meanings of the world are the constructed ones: the
"dear-this," the "enemy-this," the memory and conjecture that spin out a world of separated objects,
built by the inner-self, the contracted "I."

So the collection opens with the whole picture in miniature. The own-self alone of all beings is the
one Lord. The bound one arises by the own-form-un-cognition, the many person in the round of
enjoyment. The Lord's powers appear as the world's qualities in the bound soul. And even the bound
one's world of constructed objects, even the void, is grounded in the Lord's non-conventional
this-ness. All the categories, all the knowers, rest in the one free Lord — and this is the foundation
on which the recognition of liberation will be built.

**The bond and the liberation: how the bound creates, and how he is freed**

We come now to the heart of the matter: the essence of the knower, the known, the bond, and the
liberation. The great question is how the bound knower relates to the Lord. For the bound one does not
merely suffer the world; he *creates* it, after his own fashion. But his creation is not the Lord's.

The bound one's creation is *un-common* (asādhāraṇī) — it is private, his own, per-knower and
per-moment, vanishing with him. Yet it does not stand on its own: it is *sustained by the Lord's
creation* (īśasṛṣṭyujīvinī), riding on the back of the reality that the Lord alone makes. The objection
arises: "if the paśu creates, is his creation not common, like the Lord's?" No. The paśu's own power is
hidden from him — he is other-dependent — and only the Lord-ness can awaken it. The whole difference of
bound and liberated hangs on a single fact: the bound one does not *know* his own power. He forgets
that the world he builds is built with the Lord's own materials. The māyā-power, the word-mass of the
Lord, the wheel of the syllable-deities, the eight-fold class — all this moves through him like the
rising and falling of the breath, and makes the "friend-this, enemy-this" constructions of his little
world. Even his wildest creations — the ten-tusked elephant of his fancy — are only rearrangements of
appearances the Lord has made.

The construction-action, then, is the bond. It is of the breath-form, ever-moving, and it exists
precisely to obstruct the bound one's rest. By it the māyā-power binds the animal. Even the seemingly
free constructions — "I, the king, stand," "I have slain my enemy" — are, on inspection, other-
dependent; the bound one's freedom is only apparent, resting on the Lord's. And this is the māyā in its
threefold working: the appearance of the void, the appearance of the opposite, the mere negation — all
spreading through the three stains.

Against this stands the Lord's own creation. It is *common* (sādhāraṇā) and clear-manifestation —
never constructed, always whole. And there is a path out of the bound one's prison: the abandonment of
construction. When, by the thinning of the constructions and the gathering of the mind to one point,
the bound one comes to the "I-this" of the Lord, his animal-ness is destroyed and the Lord-ness shines.
Even the animal's own creation, if it is known in the light of the Lord's power, becomes common and
real. The whole practice — the one-pointedness, the cultivation — is the letting-go of the constructions
that bind.

And this is the recognition. The world-self — the very one who is the grasper and the grasped, the
manifestation and its mass — that one is the "I." The Lord is not another; he is the "aham" of every
"aham." When the constructions fall into the great re-recollection, they cease to construct; they
become the non-construction, the pure recognition. The bound one sees that he was never bound — that
all along he was the Lord, playing at finitude as a king plays at being a soldier.

What, then, of the known? The known — the objects of the world — is common: the same for the bound and
the liberated. But they know it differently. The liberated one knows it *with the non-difference of his
own self*: he knows the whole knower-group, from the pure realm down to the embryo, as "I-this," one
flavor, un-divided. The bound one knows it in the reversal, as utterly other, divided into things.
The known is the same; the knowing is not.

But in the supreme Śiva — the highest — there is no separate known at all. In the pure realm there is
a known-order; in the while-living-liberated there is; but in the parama-Śiva, the "I"-experience is
filled and nothing stands over against it. It is the consciousness-bliss-mass, the supreme, beyond all
syllables. There is no object there, because there is no otherness there.

And the fruit of the whole teaching is this: knowing one's own self as the Lord-form, seeing the
knowledge and the action as his powers, one knows and does whatever one wishes. Such a one is the
while-living-liberated, the jīvanmukta, who at the fall of the body is simply the supreme Lord. Even
the world of māyā is, in truth, the manifestation of consciousness, untouched by place and time; even
here the Lord is present. The liberation, then, is not the acquisition of something new — it is the
recognition of what one always was. The bond is the forgetting; the liberation is the recognition.

[chunk-v3-p-tattva-caturtho-close-k1-3-v49] **The closing sum: the recognition, and the end of the whole teaching**

We come to the end. This final vimarśa of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī is the closing sum — the
drawing together of everything that has gone before. And its theme is fittingly the *transmission* of
the teaching itself: it comes from the guru, from the śāstra, and from the self.

The whole teaching — the self-manifest essence, established by the knowledge and the action, aided by
reason — has been given. Part of it comes from the self (svataḥ); part from the śāstra (śāstrataḥ);
and part must come from the guru (gurutaḥ). For even the vision of the śāstra must be carried to its
proper power by the lineage of teachers. And here Abhinavagupta is stern: "the book-studied knowledges,
without the guru-order," he warns, "practicing and teaching, ripen long in hell." The teaching must be
received from the living line — from the ādi-Śrīkaṇṭhanātha down through Durvāsa and Tryambakāditya, the
mental sons who carry the un-precedented, effort-less word.

And now the path itself. Abhinavagupta presents it as a "new, well-fitted path," spoken by the great
gurus in the Śivadṛṣṭi. It is the path of the recognition. Since liberation is from the recognition
alone, all the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here; this is the clear means, effort-less,
un-undertaken, yet bearing the great fruit. The breath-controls and the rest are artificial; the
un-made reality does not yield to a sixteenth part of such effort. Even the proud fancies of the bound
— "I am the king," "I have slain my enemy" — are, when examined, still other-dependent, riding on the
Lord's power. The recognition cuts through all of it. And its fruit is the while-living-liberated, the
jīvanmukta: the one who, even in the body, is already free, and who at the fall of the body is simply
the supreme Lord. This, Abhinavagupta says, is the most wondrous thing of all — liberation in this very
life.

The closing sum puts it in a beautiful image. The lover stands near, sought by the slender woman; but
as long as he is not recognized, he cannot be enjoyed. So the world-Lord — always present, always near —
is not experienced in his own splendor until the recognition arises. The world has him before it, and
yet does not see him, until the single act of recognition turns the un-known nearness into the joy of
union. One who knows only the mere flash of recognition gains the bliss; one who cultivates it gains
the thousand-fold embrace.

And this recognition, Abhinavagupta reminds us, was established for the world by Utpala — "the sun-rise
son" — for the effort-less establishment of all people, not by caste or conduct but by the very fact of
being born a knower. Through it, all beings are graced; and by it, the author himself is complete. The
whole teaching — the Lord's recognition — is here gathered and handed on.

The closing vimarśa then turns to the author's own lineage — the vivṛtikāra's seventeen verses of
praise. They trace the line: Varāha-gupta, the Cukhulaka, father of Bhūtirāja; Bhūtirāja himself;
Haṭitalakṣmaṇagupta, the maker of the śāstra, the guru of Abhinava; the Tryambaka with its three
powers; and the method of the recognition throughout. The final verses praise the supreme Lord and
hand the work to him: "the Lord-recognition, from the reflective-awareness of the Lord, may he make it
the one minding the self's reflection." And then the two colophons close the entire work: the
"all-conclusion, the fourth vimarśa"; and "completed — this, the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī, the
composition of the Abhinavagupta-foots, whose fame is won by meditation on the feet of Tri-nayana."

So ends the greatest work of Abhinavagupta — the Vivṛtivimarśinī on the recognition of the Lord. It
has traced, across four adhikāras, the knowledge and the action of consciousness, the categories of
the world, the knowers and the stains, the bond and the liberation. And it closes where it began: the
own-self of all beings is the one Lord, and the recognition of this — received from the guru, the
śāstra, and the self — is the whole of liberation. The book ends, and the recognition begins.
